speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of immediate and pressing necessity to move a motion having to do with the crippling effects which the recent freight rate increases have placed upon the livestock and meat processing industry of western Canada, and the failure of this government to honour its commitments to overcome freight rate discrepancies in the livestock industry which now threatens the future of this important segment of the western economy. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave):
That the federal government take immediate steps to remove the freight rate inequities existing between grain and meat shipments to central Canada: that the discriminatory gap on freight rates between processed beef and live beef be reduced to a realistic and equitable level and, further, that any freight rate increases be suspended until such corrective policies are put in place.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH COMMISSION TO REVIEW FEDERAL EXECUTIVE, LEGISLATIVE AND JUDICIAL SALARIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill would establish, for a one-year term every four years, a Federal Remuneration Review Commission to recommend appropriate remuneration for federal executive, legislative and judicial offices, to take effect from the following general election. It avoids indexation, which parliament has not endorsed for other earnings, and avoids as well the arbitrary assessment of our own worth. While recognizing the ultimate responsibility of parliament to decide on such remuneration, this bill would ensure an orderly, open, regular review on the basis of independent analysis and advice.

MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   TRANSPORT FREIGHT RATES-EFFECT OF COURT DECISION ON JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the situation resulting from the recent court decision setting aside a decision of the Canadian Transport Commission on the railways' application for freight rate increases, which raises the question of where the responsibility for regulating freight rates in this country lies and aggravates even further the inequities and anomalies which have existed for so long in our freight rate structure.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   TRANSPORT FREIGHT RATES-EFFECT OF COURT DECISION ON JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSION
speechtext:
Order. As required under the terms of Standing Order 26, the hon. member has given the Chair notice of his intention to move his motion. The question of freight rates is, of course, an extremely important one. Nevertheless, I feel compelled to rule against the introduction of the motion for two reasons. First, as appears from the terms of the hon. member's own motion, the decision to which he refers is one which aggravates a situation which has existed for a long time. I think it would be most difficult to place upon this situation, or even upon the hon. member's description of it, any interpretation which would accurately describe it as an emergency occurrence. Second, the hon. member has referred to the decision of the courts. Regardless of how it might be interpreted, this is one of a series of either judicial or semi-judicial proceedings which are taking place with respect to freight rates and in these circumstances, rather than inviting a debate in this chamber to place an interpretation upon a court decision it would seem to me that this House ought to resist getting into such an area while matters of this importance are under a judication before the courts and may continue to be before the courts or administrative bodies.
Unless I were persuaded that there would be no other way in which the House could get at this subject-and I am not-I cannot hold that we should set aside our regular

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is the minister currently exploring with the leaders of labour whether they will agree to a specific claim on the gross national product? speechtext:
I have said that
because the initial thrusts of inflation were internationally oriented, in terms of the imbalance of supply and demand, shortage of basic commodities, bad harvests and then the quadrupling of oil prices, it is now quite understandable that wage and salary rates are attempting to catch up so as to offer some sort of compensation for the erosion of income that has been suffered as a result of rising prices over the last 18 months. The problem now is that unless there is some sort of mutual understanding, not only with labour but with business, the professions, owners of rental property and other segments of the economy, there is the likelihood that wage settlements, in anticipation of a continuation of future inflation at cur-

I told the labour leaders as long as six months ago in Vancouver that from my point of view the addition of a COLA clause makes a good deal of sense, because it responds to the cost of living rather than anticipating rates of inflation, which hopefully will not be attained. Thank you, Madam Chairman. Shortly before the hour of four o'clock on Friday last I reversed mileage figures, and the sentence reported in Hansard at page 2599, toward the end of the first column, should read: We must think in terms of ... 15 to 40 miles per gallon rather than ... 6 to 12 miles per gallon.
The balance of my remarks will conclude my participation in the debate on these two paragraphs. It is still my contention that paragraphs 11 and 12 are causing hardship. One Vancouver yard has been faced with the cancellation of $500,000 of work. In addition, one half of its back orders have been cancelled. In another yard, $150,000 worth of work has been cancelled and, again, one half of the back orders cancelled. This yard is itself seeking to cancel $200,000 worth of purchase commitments placed as far away as Sydney, Nova Scotia. A $300,000 new model moulding development program has been stopped.
I would bring it to the minister's attention that Sceptre Equipment Limited, a small construction equipment company in North Vancouver, has a tax-paid D-7 and two loaders in inventory. At the time of import, $12,000 was paid in federal sales tax. The minister offers tax recovery procedures to automotive companies in similar circum-

stances, yet he digs in his heels when asked to deal with this man's problem. This man needs relief; he needs a procedure by which he can recover his $12,000 since he cannot now sell the equipment at its tax-paid value. Where is the just society, about which the Prime Minister boasts at election time, in the face of this refusal of justice on the part of the Minister of Finance?
The pleasure boat industry in British Columbia alone is a $78 million industry and the incomes of a lot of people are affected by this vindictive stroke of a bitter pen. There is no logic or justice about the minister's explanations in support of paragraphs 11 and 12 of clause 21 and the lack of procedure for recovering sales tax on inventories of construction equipment. The minister's action negates the small harbour assistance programs which are still being put into effect by other departments of government. It negates years of government programs to encourage the development of the boat building industry which is responsible for important payrolls in British Columbia. After all, British Columbia is a marine-oriented province.
The paragraphs of the bill to which I refer are highly discriminatory against a minority who as individuals make a higher than average contribution to the gross national product. The reasons given for the inclusion of paragraphs 11 and 12 do not stand up to examination. Any loss of revenue due to the abandoning of this policy could be recovered if stricter attention were given to avoiding wasteful government expenditure. As a means of conserving energy, the measures we are being asked to approve penalize only those who have been saving for their dream, not those who are already equipped with aircraft and boats. Surely, dealers with tax-paid inventories of construction equipment on hand are entitled to the same recovery procedures as are automotive dealers.
I support the amendments offered by the hon. member for Moncton and urge the minister to reconsider what appears to be an extremely rigid and autocratic stand on these three items in Bill C-40.

The purpose of these excise tax provisions is obviously to dampen down the use of energy by increasing the financial burden placed upon those who use motor boats and cars, particularly those requiring a great deal of fuel. The insertion of these clauses emphasizes the need for a comprehensive energy policy in this country. Most people would agree that the increase in the cost of running a motor boat, for example, would in theory be of some value as a measure designed to conserve fuel supplies. However, in this instance it is discriminatory. The minister might well consider explaining to the committee why he has not included snowmobiles, for example, in these provisions. After all snowmobiles, like boats, are used for pleasure. Some people in Canada find snowmobiles very important to their livelihood. It seems to me it would have been fairer to have taxed none or all of these craft used for pleasure. It is also an indication that the time has long since passed when the government should bring forward its energy policy. Like the Americans, we will have to decide how high the price of energy should go in order to implement some form of rationing and conserve fuel.

There is one other item I should like the minister to clarify regarding the tax on boats, and that is whether or not fishing boats will be taxed. I ask this because in my riding the lake fishery uses boats of a fair size, and the industry is at a rather low level. It is now being assisted by ARDA grants, the provincial government and various other programs, but placing an added tax on these boats would be an imposition upon the industry. I believe it is provided that boats used for fishing will not be taxed, but I should like to hear the minister himself directly say that this is so. I think it is most important that in general there is no excise tax on production items. For instance, I understand there is no excise tax on farm tractors, tools and other items used to produce goods. When the minister speaks perhaps he will clarify whether the clause on boats applies to fishing boats. The fishing industry is directly dependent on the use of boats as tools to enable the fishermen to earn their livelihood. With these requests, perhaps the minister in due course would answer my question regarding the tax on fishing boats.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, first of all I should like to thank the Minister of Finance for amending the Excise Tax Act last Thursday so that clause 18 now encompasses regional districts, fire districts and unorganized territories. For almost two years I have been trying to get something done about this question, and this just shows that by persistent attack we can get the finance minister to see the logic of our arguments.
The tax on boats is a very serious matter for the manufacturers of boats in Canada, as well as for those who buy and use pleasure boats. Again I would ask the minister to tell us the philosophy behind this excise tax; I have never been able to understand it. Is the government simply looking for some easy money? Do they pick on industries which they feel will be easy marks, industries in which they believe the majority of the people are not interested or about which they do not care? Perhaps they feel they should tax areas that would appeal to the public. I believe the government's thinking is that the tax on the boat industry would be a popular move from the public's point of view.
The government is trying to use the excuse of energy conservation to justify its action. It does not tell the people that really it is looking for some easy money. It is desperately looking for sources of revenue to satisfy the spending programs of money hungry government departments. Surely the minister must worry about putting people out of work. In the three years the Minister of Finance has been minister we have had one of our highest average unemployment rates. The average trade balance deficit over those three years has been close to $1 billion, whereas in the preceding three years we averaged a slight surplus. It is because these industries have been picked on that this deficit has been generated. The boat industry in Canada is not healthy; it has to compete with industries in other parts of North America which buy their components more cheaply. The Canadian boat industry has had to struggle in the past, at the best of times, without having to face an excise tax on its products.
Excise
Over 80 per cent of the boats sold in British Columbia have more than a 20 horsepower motor. The motor boat industry in Canada consumes less than 1 per cent of all gas used. This is hardly sufficient to justify an excise tax. The boat manufacturers have already been hit very hard by the energy crisis. For example, in one year the cost of resin used in making fibreglass boats has gone from 20 cents a pound to 56 cents a pound, almost three times as much. Plastic used in the upholstery of boats has risen in cost by 27 per cent. In 1973, a popular model of boat manufactured in my constituency sold for $5,847, but in 1974 it sold for $7,268. With the increase in tax proposed by the government, this boat will cost $7,915 because of the increase in tax amounting to $647.
I do not think this increase is going to deter people from buying boats. The tax on heavy cars certainly will not stop people who can afford to buy Cadillacs. This is really an additional source of revenue to the government. I hope the government will not do anything that will put the boat industry out of business, so I plead with the minister to reconsider the excise tax that he is proposing to place upon boats used for pleasure.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, when the excise tax bill we are dealing with was drafted, somebody must have been out to lunch, because they did not take into consideration the fact that in some parts of Canada boats are used for purposes other than pleasure. In my riding, boats are an essential form of transportation. As many as 30 communities in my riding do not have roads, and when you do not have roads the waterways become your avenues of travel. The people there do not have any choice in respect of paying this 10 per cent excise tax: they cannot say they will not buy a boat, because they require a boat as an essential means of travel. The government should seriously consider giving people in remote areas some sort of tax concession, because while these boats could be classed as pleasure boats, they really are not because they are essential to these communities. There is hardly a person in these remote areas who has a boat with a motor of less than 20 horsepower, and therefore they are subject to this 10 per cent tax. There are also a number of commercial fishermen in my area, and they use boats extensively. I should like to know whether they will be exempt from this 10 per cent tax.
We should also take a serious look at this 10 per cent tax on aircraft. The people who own aircraft in my constituency do not use them strictly for pleasure; many of them operate small lodges and use small aircraft to haul groceries to outlying stores. I repeat that the area I represent does not have an extensive roads system and many of the people who live there must rely on aircraft to get supplies to their operations. I am talking about the small operator who uses a 180-Cessna and hauls groceries 200 miles to supply a store in a remote area. I see the minister is agreeing with me, so I hope there will be action soon in this regard.
We must also be very careful when imposing these taxes on people in the remote parts of Canada. Yesterday I said that many jobs remained unfilled in northern Manitoba. Perhaps this is because of the high cost of living in the remote parts of the country. We are now preparing to

Excise
impose an additional charge, in the form of this excise tax, on equipment that is essential to the survival of people in northern Manitoba. It is about time somebody-and I hope to do this-brought to the attention of the rest of Canada and the government the situation that exists in northern Manitoba.
If the government insists on imposing taxes of this kind, I am afraid we will find that the natural resources we are trying to harvest in northern Manitoba will not be harvested: people will not be able to afford to harvest them. If we want to encourage people to work in the remote areas of Canada, we must provide some incentive. There is certainly no incentive to anyone to go into the north, particularly for the first time, when he is faced with having to purchase a boat for transportation, or perhaps an aircraft, and has to pay this 10 per cent tax. To me this tax is ridiculous.
The other matter I want to talk about is the tax on air transportation. This has caused untold hardship for the small air carriers in northern Manitoba. speechtext:
Madam Chairman, when speaking on Bill C-40 it is difficult to add very much on the subject of boats since so much has already been said. One thing that does strike me is that we are adding a tax on top of a tax. This means that the treasury department of the government will be making more profit from these transactions than will the manufacturer or his employees, the wholesaler or distributor or their employees, or the retailer or his employees.
At a time when retail sales are lagging, employees of retailers are being laid off or are working shorter hours. Retailers and wholesalers are facing cutbacks and a reduction in profits. Approximately 23 per cent of their profit goes to the government for little or no input-certainly no useful input. Retailers and wholesalers who could go bankrupt in transactions such as this, and in fact have been known to go bankrupt, receive little or no sympathy. Nevertheless, the government still gets its pound of flesh.
Madam Chairman, I wonder if I might ask you to call to order hon. friends to my left who are being particularly noisy this afternoon, all three of them. One of them is perhaps the instigator, but all three are noisy.
The money that is received from these taxes is going into the government's coffers. What is the government going to do with all the money it has collected? What has the government done with money collected from similar taxes in the past? I suggest that the answer is that they have done very little, certainly very little of interest to the manufacturers of boats, to the wholesalers, distributors and retailers of boats, and a whole lot less to the owners of boats. These boats provide pleasure to many families in what is commonly called the middle class. These people, who already bear a major portion of the tax load in this country, are sometimes called the silent majority. Perhaps they are the ones who most need a break on a Saturday or Sunday afternoon to get away from some of the pressures imposed by this government. I strongly suggest to the minister that he consider a break for these people. He would not be giving anything away, but merely reducing the load that is already on them.
I want to add a few words with regard to private business aircraft. I think it has been firmly established that the amount of fuel used by this type of aircraft is absolutely minimal in comparison with the consumption of energy in the country. In a country as vast as Canada, aircraft are an essential means of transportation for businessmen. Many people may look on this, and perhaps the minister does, as taxing the rich who can afford it. But I say to the minister that this is not so. Certainly, the majority of aircraft owners pay perhaps more than the
January 28, 1975

average corporate or personal income tax, and their aircraft help them to increase their revenue and consequently the amount of tax they pay. So why should the government not pass legislation to encourage businessmen to continue earning more money? The government cannot have it both ways. These people are frequently capable of providing new jobs for many Canadians, and they should be encouraged to do so.
The arguments that have been put forward regarding fuel savings, I consider to be hogwash and balderdash, or whatever strong term is allowed within the procedures of this august body. This is a measure to give the illusion of taxing the rich. The government could easily save far more energy in any one of the dozen ways suggested by the Minister of Public Works, and impose any other method of taxation. But the answer is really to curtail government spending in many areas that have already been suggested. In my opinion, the government has tried many other ways to discourage businessmen in Canada from using private aircraft, yet this is a form of transportation that should not be discouraged.
Together with my colleagues on this side of the House and many hon. members on the other side, I ask the minister to give serious consideration to rescinding these two paragraphs which would do much harm to a viable industry.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I want to deal with clause 21, more specifically paragraph 7 of Part XVII, having to do with the following vehicles:
Air cushion vehicles and tracked vehicles specially designed to transport twelve or more passengers or ten thousand pounds or more freight.
I will deal with tracked vehicles designed to transport
10,000	pounds or more freight. I wonder why the limit was set at 10,000 pounds rather than a lower figure that could meet the same purposes. I think, of course, that the purpose is to prevent the exemptions from applying to vehicles used for recreational purposes or pleasure.
But, there is already a major company here in Canada- Bombardier-that already manufactures tracked vehicles designed to transport 8,000 pounds of freight. Those vehicles are quite popular, and it is well known that the fact that they can transport 8,000 pounds of freight stops them from being considered as purely recreational vehicles.
May I be allowed, Madam Chairman, to point out to the minister that there might be grounds to consider seriously amending paragraph 7 and reduce from 10,000 to 8,000 pounds the transportation capacity of tracked vehicles because Bombardier is the biggest manufacturer in the world of tracked vehicles, whether pleasure or industrial vehicles. There are no known recreational vehicles transporting more than 2,000 pounds of freight at present. Bombardier now manufactures the Muskeg Carrier, a vehicle that is sold to industry only. The Muskeg Carrier can transport a maximum of 8,000 pounds of freight. It is priced at $20,000. It is surely not a vehicle designed for pleasure or recreational purposes.
In my opinion, this bill as it now stands prompts prospective customers to buy much heavier vehicles than might be required under present standards. Businessmen
Excise
would thus be encouraged to buy much heavier tracked vehicles precisely to avoid that tax, and this legislation would therefore be detrimental to a major industry which has been manufacturing vehicles with an 8,000 lb. carrying capacity and designed for industrial purposes.
The Bombardier Corporation which employs thousands of people in Canada manufactures vehicles specifically designed for industrial purposes. The vehicle I have been talking about, namely the Muskeg Carrier has an 8,000 lb. capacity. The only other industrial vehicle they manufacture has a 30,000 lb. carrying capacity.
For all those reasons, and I believe it is fair to say that the 10,000 lb. limit was specified for the sole purpose of preventing vehicles which are used for recreational purposes to benefit from the exemption, I think there would be no harm in amending section 7 and lowering the limit from 10,000 to 8,000 lbs. At all events, this would help an important industry which already manufactures tracked vehicles designed for the transportation of goods. It would be beneficial to the purchasers of those vehicles without being detrimental to anybody, and I think the legislator's purpose would be met because the exemption would apply to a vehicle which is really designed for industrial transportation. The limit should be lowered to 8,000 lbs.
Madam Chairman, I wish the minister would seriously consider those few remarks which I hope will be fruitful. An amendment aimed at reducing to 8,000 lbs. the limit provided in section 7 of part XVII should be moved.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, it is my pleasure to follow a member of the government who has lent his voice to the representations being made to the minister for amendments to Bill C-40 with regard to the discriminatory tax proposed therein. It is with interest that I see members of the government using this forum to impress upon the minister the fact that changes will have to be made to the bill. Many of the things we are saying may be repetitious, but even with my limited experience I can see that a lot of repetition is needed before this government listens.
This government, and especially the Minister of Finance, remind me of the tax collectors of medieval times. Perhaps the best thing that could be said for them is that they were quite innovative in their methods. They must have spent all their time trying to devise new means of collecting taxes from citizens. I am rather hesitant to mention any examples of that time for fear the minister might introduce some of them. History teaches us that a number of rulers, especially Peter the Great, brought in a so-called beard tax. He thought every man should be clean-shaven, but if they insisted on wearing beards when they visited the cities or towns, they were taxed for the privilege. There were other innovations, too. Now that I have cited one example, I wonder if the minister is going to ask each of my colleagues who wears a beard to pay a tax every time he comes into the House. Maybe he should start with the Secretary of State who, after some comments he made last week, seems to be trying to hide behind his beard.
Madam Chairman, in respect of the excise tax to be imposed on small aircraft, I should like to point out that

the northern half of my riding relies heavily on small aircraft for business and everyday activities such as the movement of goods and services. A number of small aircraft charter companies have built up the industry over a long period of time. The people they are serving, often the native and Metis people, are those least able to afford any increase in the cost of goods and services. In fact, the price of foodstuffs in this area is the highest in Canada at present. This excise tax will do nothing to reduce the cost of living of these people. I think the minister should re-examine this question. He is not simply taxing people who use small aircraft for pleasure but, rather, those who can least afford it. The costs of operating small aircraft have increased astronomically in the past year.
This may seem to be a relatively insignificant clause in the bill, but nevertheless we should examine it carefully. One or two small businessmen in my riding have become involved in the sale and service of small aircraft in the last few years. Lower overhead costs have enabled them to compete with larger companies but, of course, as their volume of sales dwindles they will be strapped for funds; and that is what will happen as a result of this tax. One owner of a small company in my riding recently explained to me the way he acquired aircraft and sold them and the difficulties he would face. For the protection of small businesses I think the minister should re-examine this clause.
The effect of the excise tax on boats owned by people in the northern part of my riding will be much the same. The minister received a letter dated November 20, 1974, from the Allied Boating Association of Canada. I am sure he has read the letter. Some hon. members may have quoted this letter already, but I think it bears repeating because of its significance to my riding. It is addressed to the Minister of Finance and it reads:
Dear Sir:
On behalf of the pleasure boat industry in Canada, we strenuously object to the special excise tax for pleasure boats and engines in your budget speech of November 18, 1974.
The inclusion of pleasure craft and outboard motors in your "High energy consumer" category is, in our opinion, a gross misrepresentation of fact. The annual boating consumption of gasoline is about one-half of 1 per cent of that used by Canadian automobiles.
The salient facts are:
1.	Boats are not, in general, large energy consumers.
2.	Marine manufacturers, dealers, marina and service facilities are usually a small business operation.
3.	Our industry appears to have been the hardest hit in the new excise taxes.
4.	At least 80 per cent of the boat sales dollars will be affected.
5.	Order cancellations have already been received by manufacturers as a result of the November 18 speech.
6.	The resulting vastly increased sales price will add to inflation.
We emphasize that your new excise tax of 10 per cent for boats and engines is discriminatory, unfair and presents a serious threat to the small boat industry in Canada. Your attention to eliminate this tax is urgently requested.
The letter is signed by Mr. Don J. Critton, president, Allied Boating Association of Canada. Madam Chairman, the points made by the writer are valid for any part of Canada where small boats are manufactured and used in the pursuit of private enterprise. In my riding, the G. H. Lund Boat Company Limited was established two or three years ago. The parent company is in the United States. I

am not one of those members who cringe at the prospect of American investment in my riding; indeed, I think if we can co-operatively develop an industry and provide work for the people of the riding, then their investment is welcome.
This company approached the citizens of Steinbach and asked if they were interested in a boat manufacturing company being established in the town, and if labour was available. The company wanted to build a plant which would manufacture light aluminum boats mainly for the western Canadian market. After holding discussions with members of the community, the principals of the company applied for a Department of Regional Economic Expansion grant, which was subsequently approved and received.
The company invested money in Steinbach. Local townspeople were approached and asked if they, too, wanted to invest in the company. They bought shares in the company, and its success story is remarkable. Because of good management, because the market was looked into carefully, this company is a success. Today it competes with American manufacturers. Eastern Canadian manufacturers have always found it difficult to compete in this area simply because extra freight charges are imposed on light boats of the kind manufactured by the company. The Steinbach company has expanded and has recently gone into fibreglass boat manufacturing. To me, this is a success story. Local people invested in the company and the company is a good corporate citizen, having become an integral part of the community. It is a member of the Allied Boating Association of Canada which recently made representations on behalf of this company, as well as on behalf of others, about the proposed excise tax. The general manager and vice-president of the company wrote a letter to the Minister of Finance dated November 25, 1974, which reads:
Dear Sir:
As a new manufacturer of pleasure boats in Manitoba, we endorse completely the letter of protest sent to you under date of November 20, 1974, by the Allied Boating Association of which we are members.
The pleasure boat industry in Canada from the manufacturer through to the dealer falls into the category of small business which, I submit, is less able to absorb a tax of the magnitude proposed. Boating in Canada utilizes a lower volume of energy fuel per dollar of manufacturing than do many other industries in Canada, and we therefore submit that the excise tax proposed is discriminatory.
Your review of the proposed excise tax in relation to the revenue to be derived for the federal government measured against the losses suffered by the industry as a whole and the loss of corporate tax revenues which will undoubtedly follow is requested-
The letter is signed by Mr. G. V. Hastings, general manager and vice-president. The point has not been made sufficiently that this industry consumes far less energy than most other industries of similar size. 1 will not belabour the point. As this industry is competing successfully with boating manufacturers of the United States and eastern Canada, and as the government wants to encourage economic activity in designated areas, I ask the minister and his departmental officials, on behalf of my constituents, to consider our representations seriously and objectively, in the hope that the tax to be imposed will be fair and will not militate against the best interests of all.

Madam Chairman, may I draw the minister's attention to clause 21(8). I am concerned about the proposed reduction of sales tax on construction materials. The question I raise deals specifically with the financial repercussions of this reduction on unlicensed hardware wholesalers, of whom there are many in this country. The point is that there is a difference in the competitive positions of unlicensed hardware wholesalers and those who hold a federal licence which results directly from the way in which the tax is collected. The unlicensed hardware wholesaler buys goods for resale and pays his supplier the applicable federal sales tax on building materials, which before November 18, 1974, was 11 per cent or 12 per cent. Since he pays his tax money directly to the supplier or manufacturer, the tax becomes part of his direct cost and is included in the cost of his inventory.
The licensed hardware wholesaler, on the other hand, is in exactly the same business as his unlicensed counterpart, but holds a federal sales tax licence which allows him to buy goods from the same source that his unlicensed counterpart buys from. He, however, does not pay tax at the time of purchase but, rather, collects the federal sales tax applicable when he sells those goods and then remits
Excise
the tax. In other words, the licensed hardware wholesaler is a tax collector; he works under the advantage that the cost of his inventory does not include federal sales tax, an advantage not to be discounted lightly in view of the present cost of money. With regard to the budget and the reduction of the sales tax from 11 or 12 per cent to 5 per cent, quite frankly this has put the unlicensed hardware wholesaler in a tremendously non-competitive position vis-a-vis his licensed wholesaler counterpart. It will remain this way until stocks have been turned over and the two start off on an equal footing. Approximately 30 per cent of the unlicensed wholesaler's stock has been depreciated through no fault of his own by the 6 per cent reduction in the sales tax.
The ramifications of this tax reduction are quite apparent as far as the competitive position of the Canadian unlicensed wholesaler is concerned and his tremendous loss in actual inventory dollars. I mention this because there are a great many more unlicensed hardware wholesalers in this country than those who hold federal wholesale licences. This large number of small, unlicensed wholesalers makes up a very significant part of small business throughout Canada. These small businesses are struggling to survive because of the competition of large conglomerates. Anything that affects them in the way this reduction in tax does, makes their survival much more difficult.
I am asking the Minister of Finance to seriously consider, on a one-shot basis, some means of compensating these unlicensed hardware wholesalers for the losses they will have to absorb on tax-paid inventory when the tax on building materials is reduced from 11 or 12 per cent to 5 per cent. I hope the minister will take that into consideration when considering clause 21(8).

Since we have been on clause 21 for some time, Madam Chairman, I thought I might make some reference to what has been said and give some response to it. I have listened with considerable interest to the comments which have been made thus far concerning Bill C-40, and particularly to the generally constructive criticism made in reference to clause 21 of the bill. I would like to assure the committee that I am sympathetic to many of the important points which have been raised, and I would like to comment on these matters at this time.
Several members said that the proposed specia< excise taxes on energy-consuming vehicles will have only a slight impact on energy conservation. It should be emphasized that the proposed taxes on energy-consuming vehicles constitute one of several programs the government has introduced to deal with the critical question of conserving Canada's energy resources. Other measures include the government's recent announcement to dramatically reduce exports of Canadian oil and petroleum products. In addition, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will shortly be bringing forward important energy conservation proposals.
It is clear that the government has little alternative but to take action today in order to minimize the future disruption which will occur as world energy reserves continue to decline. Parenthetically, I draw to the attention of the committee the fulsome measures proposed by the President of the United States to Congress that are going to have dramatic effects on energy consumption and on recreational use of energy in the United States. Although the proposed special excise taxes constitute a modest step in the direction of a more responsible allocation of scarce energy resources, the government is aware that the impact of the new taxes on industries directly affected will result in some short-term dislocations in those industries. However, it must be emphasized that disruptions in industries directly related to the consumption of petroleum products will inevitably occur, and the government must take action now to encourage such industries and consumers to adjust their production and consumption in the direction of more conservative energy-consuming products if even greater dislocations are to be avoided.
Although the purpose of the special excise taxes on the specified categories of energy-consuming vehicles is the

same-that is, to deter wasteful energy consumption-the proposed taxes as they apply to each category are quite different and it would be difficult to make any meaningful, direct comparisons between the categories. The general principle operative within each category is that items designed to consume fuel for relatively more essential purposes are excluded from the tax, whereas items which are considered to be less essential are subject to the tax.
A number of comments have been raised concerning the proposed special excise tax on motors larger than 20 horsepower and boats designed to be propelled by such motors. With regard to comments concerning the impact of the proposed tax on commercial fishermen and ferry boat operations, it should be noted that Bill C-40 provides in clause 21(2), line 40, page 11, that all boats, motors, cars and planes for which relief is provided from the general 12 per cent federal sales tax will not be subject to the proposed special excise taxes on energy-consuming vehicles.
For example, part XI of schedule III to the Excise Tax Act provides exemption from federal sales tax for boats purchased by commercial fishermen. In addition, this part provides that all ships licensed to engage in the Canadian coasting trade-for example, ferry boats used in British Columbia, the maritimes and other parts of the country- are exempt from the 12 per cent sales tax. Consequently, such boats and ships would be exempt from the proposed special excise taxes.
A number of important points were raised concerning the impact of the proposed tax on Canada's boat building and tourist industries. Since the ways and means motion was tabled in the House on November 18, 1974, the government has received a number of representations from all sectors of the boating industry. As a matter of fact, I have had several meetings, now, with representatives of the industry. These have made it clear that the economic situation of the industry has changed appreciably since the proposed taxes were first introduced in the budget of May 6. As a consequence of the extraordinary oil price increases which have occurred in the course of the last year, the industry has already experienced extremely large increases in the price of fibreglass, the principal construction material which it uses. These price increases are themselves a significant deterrent to the pruchase of high energy-consuming boats. I believe this fact, coupled with the current economic situation in the industry, warrants Bill C-40 being amended to exclude boats from the proposed special excise tax.

Questions have been raised concerning who will be permitted to purchase aircraft without paying the special excise tax. Bill C-40 gives authority to the governor in council to exclude a broad range of end users from paying the proposed tax. For greater clarity, it is intended that the governor in council should by regulation exclude aircraft from the tax as follows: (a) aircraft used in scheduled and unscheduled commercial air service to provide public transportation of persons, goods or mail both inside and outside of Canada as included in classes 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9-2, 9-3 and 9-4 of the air carrier regulations.

And 9-5. Then (b) aircraft for use exclusively in commercial flying club air services as provided in class 6 of the air carrier regulations; (c) aircraft for use exclusively in the provision of such commercial air services as specified in class 7 of the air carrier regulations whether such services are performed by licensed air carriers or not. For example; (1) agricultural flying including the application and distribution of chemicals, aerial pest control, spraying, seeding, cattle spotting, forest cultivation and fish cultivation; (2) aerial construction including aerial hoisting, pole setting and power line construction; (3) aerial control including firefighting, fire prevention, water pumping, forest control; (4) aerial inspection reconnaissance including aerial patrol and inspection, ice reconnaissance, forest, pipeline and power line patrol; (5) aerial photography and survey; (6) flying training. And (d) aircraft used exclusively to provide air services directly related to the exploration and development of natural resources in Canada; (e) police and military aircraft.
The relief from tax in respect of many of the specialty air services just described will be extended to any craft used for these purposes when owned by an individual or a commercial air service. Questions were raised concerning the position of aircraft used in a combination of exempt and non-exempt uses. It should be noted that Bill C-40 provides, in clause 13(2), that in the event an aircraft purchased under exempt conditions is diverted to a taxable use, the aircraft will become subject to tax. However, provision is made in the same clause for diversions of a casual nature which will not jeopardize the exempt status of the aircraft. The government is aware of the importance of aircraft in Canada and will take any necessary steps to ensure that the proposed tax does not exert an adverse impact on the provision of essential air services. In this regard, consultations with the general aviation industry are now under way to explore the most appropriate scope for exemptions from the proposed tax.
Comments were made by some members to the effect that smaller aircraft achieve a gas mileage comparable to
Excise
that of larger automobiles. While this may be true in some instances, the argument is not relevant for purposes of the special excise tax. To the extent that the proposed tax stimulates the utilization of existing commercial air services, more efficient energy consumption will be achieved. In response to comments that adequate commercial air services are not available to certain points in Canada, I would point out that persons flying to such points in taxable aircraft would likely be pursuing business interests and that such persons would benefit from two important tax concessions which greatly minimize the impact of the proposed tax. First, persons utilizing private aircraft for business purposes escape payment of the 5 per cent air transportation tax. Assuming a six-passenger aircraft which makes ten trips per month and has a ten-year life, the total tax savings would amount to $36,000. Second, private aircraft purchases for business purposes are deductible for purposes of corporation income tax. Assuming a 47 per cent rate for income tax, the 10 per cent special excise tax would be reduced to an effective 5.3 per cent.
I should like to conclude my remarks concerning the impact of the proposed special excise tax on Canada's aviation industry by pointing out that the November 18 budget also proposed that the 12 per cent federal sales tax be removed from aircraft used for most commercial purposes. In addition, such aircraft will not be subject to the special excise tax of 10 per cent. The removal of the 12 per cent tax will save aviation industries an estimated $20 million annually, whereas the proposed special excise tax on privately-owned aircraft will generate less than $5 million annually.
I turn, now, to the proposal to remove federal sales tax from transportation equipment. The hon. member for Hal-ton-Wentworth raised the question whether the principle of aggregate pricing would be accepted with respect to the $1,000 value per unit for parts and equipment for transportation equipment. I can assure the committee that where a manufacturer sells an assembly of parts-for example, a hydraulic tailgate-the assembly will be regarded as a unit and will qualify for the exemption as long as the price of the complete assembly exceeds $1,000. The hon. member for Halton-Wentworth also made reference to repair and replacements parts for transportation equipment and for construction equipment, suggesting that the provisions in respect of construction equipment were more generous than those accorded transportation equipment. I should like to emphasize that even though the provisions related to parts for construction equipment are worded somewhat differently from those applicable to transportation equipment, the exemptions are identical; that is, all parts for equipment valued at more than $1,000 per unit are exempt from sales tax whether for use in relation to transportation equipment or construction equipment.
While the aggregate principle to which I have just referred will be accepted in instances where manufacturers combine parts into a unit, it has come to my attention that a number of operations are out in the equipping of transportation equipment by persons who are not licensed manufacturers, and that such persons may be placed at a competitive disadvantage as a consequence of the $1,000 limit. In order to eliminate this anomaly, I propose to amend clause 21(7) to provide exemption from sales tax

January 28, 1975
Excise
for all parts and equipment installed on tax exempt transportation equipment prior to the first use of such equipment. A somewhat more significant anomaly exists with respect to the $1,000 limit as it applies to parts for aircraft. Consequently, I am proposing an amendment to remove the $1,000 limit for parts and equipment in respect of aircraft. This amendment is necessary to eliminate the possibility of conferring a competitive advantage in favour of foreign aircraft and air engine overhaul operations. A number of members on my side of the House have made this point to me, including my colleague the Minister of National Defence.
During the debate, some members observed that the special excise taxes on heavy cars proposed in the November 18 budget should apply only to vehicles ordered on or after November 19, 1974. I appreciate that there may be instances where dealers have entered into contracts with customers on or before November 18 and that in instances where those orders were not completed until after November 18 they would be subject to the special excise tax on heavy cars. It should be noted, however, that it is customary for changes in taxes on commodities, including the special excise taxes and taxes on liquor and tobacco, to come into effect on the day following the budget announcement. If this were not done, retailers and wholesalers could purchase very large quantities in advance of the tax increase and so avoid the additional tax for a time. Those with adequate cash or credit could take advantage of the delay to a greater extent than others.
In this regard, I might also point out that the special excise tax on heavy cars was first proposed in the May 6 budget. Following the defeat of the budget, a press release was issued stating that, if re-elected, it was the government's intention to ask parliament to enact legislation implementing the proposals contained in the May 6 budget. It would seem that any persons who might be subject to the proposed tax on heavy cars would have had ample time to arrange their affairs in anticipation of the new tax.
Turning briefly to the proposed reduction of federal sales tax on a comprehensive list of construction materials and equipment for buildings, I would like to emphasize that it is intended that the reduced rate of tax apply to a broad spectrum of materials and equipment. In this regard, questions were raised concerning the inclusion of free-standing fireplaces in the schedule subject to the reduced rate of tax. I would like to assure the committee that the government is prepared to review the question of including additional items in the schedules subject to the 5 per cent rate of tax. This can be accomplished by regulation of the governor in council pursuant to section 24 of part I and section 5 of part III of the proposed new schedule V to the Excise Tax Act.
Before tabling the amendments referred to earlier, I would like to comment on one other matter mentioned during the debate. This concerns comments related to the review of the commodity tax system. I wish to announce that a general review of the commodity tax system will shortly be initiated. I will be making a more detailed statement concerning this matter later in the session. At 
that time I will outline a timetable for taxpayer participation in this review.

CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO RESTRICT USE OF ABORTION PROCEDURES
speechtext:
that Bill C-219, to amend the Criminal Code (abortion), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said; Mr. Speaker, it was with some reservations that I decided to move the adoption of the bill sponsored in the twenty-ninth parliament by Mr. Don Blenkarn. I was hesitant to do so, not because I doubt the morality or justice of the legislation-I believe in it deeply-but because I know that doing so will result in my being caricatured as inhumane, repressive, insensitive, or a religious zealot. To speak of the sanctity of all human life, born or unborn, is not an acceptable action among much of our intellectual community, and I am saddened because I know that my participation in a controversy so laden with emotion will not be understood by many Canadians. I know, too, that my private member's bill will not be allowed to reach a vote and that the government will not allow any legislation of this nature to become law in Canada.
I am moving second reading of this legislation, aware of the consequences of my action but also acutely aware of the heavy personal responsibility, both as an individual and as a member of parliament, to speak as forcefully as I can against the tendency to dehumanize modern life. I rise to speak today not because I am confident that if I do so we can reverse the course of our society, but because I am fearful that if people who share a reverence for human life do not speak, our cause is certainly lost.
Abortion
The brilliant Irish poet and statesman, William Butler Yeats, believed that what he described as our present Christian, civilized age would come to an end with this century, replaced by 2,000 years of brutality and inhumanity. I remember reading once that he said the change would follow a period when people did things "not because they would or should, but because they could"; in short, when our social and mechanical technology had triumphed over our morality.
The proponents of abortion talk of its safety and relative ease: indeed, they sometimes speak of statistics which show that it is safer for a woman to abort her child than to carry him to term. They speak of the unborn child as nothing more than tissue and they euphemistically talk of "terminating pregnancy". The pro-abortionists contrast this surgical procedure which they consider safe, simple, and morally insignificant with the horrors of back-alley butchery, unwanted children and population explosion. That they are sincere, and that they fervently believe in the justice and the necessity of their cause, I do not question. I have had the opportunity to speak with many of them and I believe that they are unfairly pictured as bloodthirsty and murderous. The word "murder" to my mind implies an awareness and deliberation in the commission of evil, and they are anything but aware of the implication of their actions. Instead, I believe they are tragically mistaken about the nature of their activities.
Mr. Speaker, one of the most disturbing tendencies I have detected since coming to parliament is our anxious avoidance of attempting to resolve issues which are moral in nature. We seem to want to find technological solutions to moral dilemmas or to find compromises that leave us all feeling a little unclean but that will defuse a contentious issue. All too often we simply wash our hands of trying to find a resolution to moral problems.
The debate on capital punishment exemplified the worst of what parliament is capable of. Faced with the need to make a decision on the morality of the government in taking the lives of human beings, the legislation we settled upon satisfied neither the retentionists nor the abolitionists. What it did was to extend for another five years a partially retentionist bill that the government gives every indication of simply not enforcing.
The present abortion legislation is a classic case of an unenforceable and morally indefensible law. It satisfies neither the proponents of unlimited abortion nor those who are pro-life. What it does is to put an impediment, which is far from insurmountable, between some pregnant women and the abortion they want. It is discriminatory in that the application of the law varies widely throughout Canada, and it is almost impossible to enforce as the key provision-the health of the mother-is subject to so many different interpretations; and, of course, it fails totally to come to grips with the question of the humanity of the fetus.
The critical change which would be made if the legislation I am proposing were to pass is that it would delete references to the health of the mother and permit abortion only where a choice had to be made between the life of the mother and that of the child. In practice, it would dramati-

January 28, 1975
Abortion
cally reduce the number of abortions taking place from its current level of between 40,000 and 50,000 each year. The premise upon which the bill is based, that human life begins at conception and that all human life is precious and irreplaceable, must be addressed in any attempt to deal with the morality of abortion.
The supporters of abortion on demand must either deny the very humanity of the unborn or they must establish that some human beings are innately less human than others and that their claim to human rights is also inferior. In either case, the implications of accepting the assumptions of the pro-abortionists are horrifying because they involve the need to put a restrictive definition on what constitutes humanity and they open the door wide for the destruction of life they feel is less than human.
Are we, as a society, to define humanity on the basis of viability for independent life? If so, then what are the implications for the physically or mentally weak, the retarded, the paraplegic, the comatose, the newborn, the senile: are they no longer to be considered human beings possessing intrinsic human rights? Do we say, as most abortion laws say, that a fetus achieves humanity mysteriously after it has existed for a set number of weeks? If so, we must explain why we do not consider the life of the fetus to be a continuum, and how we can say that in the space of a second a fetus which does not appear to have changed physically has progressed from being a meaningless piece of tissue into a person with human rights. I say that such a position is unprovable and untenable: it constitutes nothing more than an avoidance of reality.
Are we to say that abortion does involve the destruction of human life, that it can be defended on the basis that not all human life is sacred, and that some of us can lay a greater claim to human rights than others? If so, then what is to be the basis for our allocation of human rights? Are they simply something to be distributed by legislation, subject to extension and withdrawal at the whim of government?
I believe that all people, regardless of race or religion, male or female, rich or poor, born or unborn, share a common humanity and that all of us have an equal right to life. I am convinced that the only instance in which the taking of another human life is justified is the most extreme case of self-defence. It is because of my belief in the sanctity of human life-all human life-that I remain opposed to capital punishment. It is also for that reason that I am committed to preserving the life of the unborn. What disappoints me acutely is that my colleagues to the left, who stood with me and who spoke eloquently for sparing the lives of a handful of individuals guilty of the most heinous of crimes, will now stand to support the destruction of nearly 50,000 innocent lives each year.
Let us turn to some of the arguments used by pro-abortionists to rationalize their position. We have already considered the claim that the fetus is not a human being, and that premise has two commonly heard corollaries; that to deny a woman the right to abort a fetus is to deny her the right to control her own body, and that the health or wishes of the mother are more important than the life of the child. If one accepts the contention that the fetus is a human being, it is obvious that the issue is not the right of the mother to control her own body, but whether she has

the right to kill another human being who shares her body. Similarly, it is hard to understand a claim that the fact that one person does not want another to live because to do so would be traumatizing or harmful to the financial position of a family, or even potentially damaging to the health of the mother, justifies killing.
A person would have to be totally blind or absolutely insensitive to the problems of other people to deny that giving birth to an unwanted child can be a tragedy. Certainly, I would never make such a claim. The potential for human misery is enormous and each one of us has a responsibility to lessen that misery in any way legally and morally acceptable. It is here that I break ranks with so many who oppose abortion but whose compassion does not extend beyond the fetus. But to share the agony of those who give birth to a child against their will is not to support the killing of another, innocent, human being. It is there that we must draw the line.
Another defence of abortion that is often heard is that because any law circumscribing abortion could be avoided by people with money to travel to another jurisdiction, the unequal application of a law is reason for eliminating it. Surely, though, we must realize that if an act is basically immoral each and every time it is committed, we cannot justify its unrestricted commission on the grounds that some people will be able to get away with it even when our society says it is indefensible.
The corollary of this assumption is the claim that because some women will decide to have an illegal and unsafe abortion at the hands of a criminal, we should abolish the law so they can have their abortions in safety and relative ease. But the issue is not the safety of abortion; it is the morality of abortion. And what is critical is not whether a law will be broken, but whether it is just. We know that almost any law we propose can and will be broken, but we do not often hear proposed legislation resisted in parliament because although the vast majority of Canadians will abide by the law, some people will elect to break it.
Another claim is that opponents of abortion are undemocratic, that Gallup polls show a majority of Canadians believe abortion should be a matter of personal choice. First of all, the evidence presented by polls is contradictory. As a poll released by Gallup last March shows, a significant plurality of Canadians felt an abortion was already too easy to obtain. Interestingly, the poll debunks the claim that abortion laws are a male attempt to oppress women, because some 11 per cent more women than men felt our abortion laws were already too lax. Secondly, it should be apparent to each of us that there are often great disparities between what is popular and what is right, and no poll, whether of the CMA or of the general public, can make something that was immoral one moment, moral the next.
It is disturbing that so many of the leftists who spoke for life during the capital punishment debate and who reminded the House of our duty to do what we believe is right, whether it is popular or not, now call for government by Gallup. My friends who take that position demonstrate a curious example of situation ethics where their support of a course depends more upon its acceptability to their ideological peers than upon its justice.
January 28, 1975

Another common excuse tendered in defence of abortion is that it is an effective means of birth control at a time of overpopulation. The implications of this particular suggestion are ominous because one could just as easily argue for killing old people, or criminals, or invalids, or the mentally retarded. Killing for the sake of reducing population is intolerable in a civilized society, and abortion is certainly not acceptable as a form of population control.
Finally, similar to the advocacy of abortion for population control is the claim that abortion is justified to prevent a child from being born who may be unwanted by his natural parents. To anyone who believes the fetus is a human being, abortion on these grounds is intolerable. I do not believe that anyone who seriously considers the case made by pro-abortionists can accept abortion except to save the life of the mother. However, the bill I am proposing today is not enough in itself to fight abortion. It should simply be one component in a comprehensive program. The pro-abortionists are quite right when they say that a reformed abortion law will be avoided and broken as long as pregnant women under enormous emotional pressure see abortion as their only means of escape from an intolerable situation.
If we are serious in our desire to reduce the abortion rate, and if we do have compassion for the women caught in a tragic situation, we must be willing as a society to put our money, our legislation and our moral suasion on the side of life. These are the other components of a policy which I think could reverse the direction in which we are going: first, all levels of government must co-operate in improving birth control education throughout Canada. Improved educational programs could make an attack on ignorance and would be a powerful means of reducing these human tragedies. Second, birth control devices should be made available free of charge through the medicare program to eliminate any financial disincentives to the use of contraception. Third, improved assistance should be provided to children's aid societies for their important work.
Fourth, the federal government should pressure the provinces to repeal legislation that discriminates against illegitimate children. We must recognize the equality of all children, regardless of the marital status of their parents. Fifth, society should provide every assistance possible to unwed mothers to help them over the crisis period. Instead, the harassment and discrimination against unwed mothers is enormous. We must remove the stigma from unwed motherhood, giving support to these mothers instead of making their lives more difficult.
Sixth, we should provide financial assistance to groups counselling women on the positive alternatives to abortion. At the present time, the federal government gives money to groups facilitating abortions, but it does not help those who are specifically dedicated to the reduction of abortions. Seventh, our social assistance programs should provide a decent level of assistance to needy families with children, because much of the trauma for many families involves having another child when money is scarce.
I believe that, coupled with a reform of our abortion laws, these proposals could result in a dramatic reduction
Abortion
of the innocent lives lost to abortion. I urge both sides in this debate to look beyond simply changing the laws to the need for policies that will assist thousands of human beings in difficulty. We must not allow ourselves to become so preoccupied with the debate on new legislation that we ignore the people we say we want to assist. Over the next several years parliament and the Canadian people will be faced with a series of issues that will test our national judgment. Euthanasia, genetic engineering, psychosurgery and abortion will each require us to make decisions about what makes us human beings and how we can preserve our humanity.
The application of modern technology to our social problems has had the effect of both extending our reach as individuals and depersonalizing our lives. Modern technology has extended our life spans, reduced our workload, expanded our leisure time, broadened our knowledge and increased our prosperity, but it has also eroded our sense of purpose and depersonalized our relationships with our fellow man. Even death and our attitude toward it have been changed by our modern technology. We are freed from the killer diseases that once ravaged former societies, and we take pride in having conquered nature and reducing war. But there is another side to our technological society, the cold, depersonalized, remote-control destruction of human life; and we seem to believe that antiseptic, passionless killing is a sign of how far we have progressed as a civilization.
There was an example of what I mean during the capital punishment debate when one of my colleagues proposed legislation he felt would make the killing more attractive. He would have retired the hangman's noose in favour of a simple, painless injection. And modern warfare conducted from airplanes or submarines or missile bases represents the perfection of killing by remote control. We do not have to see the people we kill, and it all seems so much less messy than before.
So it is with abortion. We do not know the fetus and we do not mourn its loss, because we have come to think of it as simply useless tissue, almost a cancer that needs to be removed. The supporters of abortion will tell you about its ease, its safety and its virtual painlessness. Abortion is fast, neat and an easy escape from our problems. Indeed, it has become so simple and acceptable that a recent study reported in the November 16, 1974, issue of the Canadian Medical Association Journal showed that experiencing a previous abortion has little effect in inducing women to adopt a more effective method of birth control.
I am deeply disturbed by the effect of abortion on the thousands of unborn children killed last year, but I am even more frightened by the effect of abortion on those of us who remain, because abortion is a denial of the sanctity of human life, a statement that our society holds life cheaply. As legislators, we hold a trust both for those who live now in our country and for those who are as yet unborn. If we are to keep that trust, it is our duty to speak in defence of human life.
Some people will have reservations about the course of action we propose because we will be called upon to make judgments which cannot be tested by computers or analysed by modern science. At times we may be mistaken. But if we are to err, let it be on the side of life; for if

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO RESTRICT USE OF ABORTION PROCEDURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always with a certain uneasiness that political bodies, made up of elected representatives, choose to deal with highly emotional issues which are the source of impassioned debates within the public. These include capital punishment, abortion, and euthanasia, because they touch on the integrety of human life and divide our society into two irreconcilable parties, made up respectively of those for and those against, which accuse each other of defending indefensible positions.
In fact, these are such highly emotional issues that people are no longer asking what your opinion is, but insist now that you take a stand. These remain however modern issues over which physicians, priests, psychologists and politicians will ponder and which a number of nations had eventually to cope with.
In addition, at this point in the history of civilization where we are starting to worry about the decreasing relation between the rate of growth of the population and that of resources, it is of the utmost importance that we should reflect as reasonable men on the means available to us for generalizing collective greater well-being.
To seek to reply positively or negatively to those questions, and more specifically to abortion, a corrective measure and no more, is to give it the value of a right, which it is not. It is rather an exceptional measure which, in some cases, can be legitimized to safeguard fundamental human rights. Once the debate is put back in its real context, the discussion can be broached with more serenity and objectivity.
The present Canadian act satisfies no one. On the one hand, for those who are in favour of it, it is too strict and it leads to discrimination. For those who are against it, it leads to scandal, to abortion on request. In fact, here again, there is need for moderation, for a study that is strictly legalistic in nature: criticism will follow automatically.
The provisions of the Canadian act on therapeutic abortion are relatively flexible. Except for that which stipulates the creation of a selection committee of three doctors, one can interpret them restrictively or very broadly. But that very flexibility has given rise to discrimination and uncertainty, for it lends itself to various interpretations and there is practically no way of knowing what intentions the legislator has, if any. Furthermore, application procedures are inadequate. In fact, as the decision depends on a committee of three doctors and they have no guidelines whatever, in accordance with the beliefs, the prejudices, the nationalities of these doctors, the therapeutic committees have interpreted the law in their own way and arbitrariness reigned.
The whole problem resides in the interpretation to be given in the legislation to the term "patient's health". Not all doctors define health in the same way. Is it the absence of disease? In other words, must we take exclusively into account psychological or physiological criteria, or must we also bear in mind psycho-social motives, including factors

such as a sufficient number of children, the advanced age of the mother, the financial situation, an unsuitable home or the fear of childbirth? The whole debate revolves around this.
The World Health Organization has replied to that question. It defines health as follows: a complete state of physical, moral and social well-being not existing solely because of an absence of disease or disability. Understanding and accepting this definition is vital if one wishes to debate abortion. Because, if we Canadians refuse to answer the question, we maintain the existing social evil of illegal abortion, and recourse to abortion abroad.
Some might say this is only an ethical problem. To me it is also-and mainly-a political problem. The aim here is not to give the woman concerned, through liberalization, a false illusion of freedom of choice. Within the present framework of our society and our laws, this would be immoral. We have here a group responsibility. When a woman comes to the point of requesting abortion, something went wrong somewhere along the line and this is our responsibility. If we favour the use of personal freedom, we should be practical about it and give each one the tools needed to use that freedom of choice. Otherwise there is no real choice. Or alternatively, we put personal freedom under the heading of collective freedom. We say no on every count, we shut our eyes, and let illegal abortionists operate. I have too much respect for human life to let
100,000	Canadian women go to charlatans each year. That is no solution. I am strongly against it and as a politician as well as a man I will not shut my eyes on the facts. As I indicated, abortion is an exceptional measure. What may then be done to prevent it? We must concentrate on prevention and information on the first hand, and help families on the other. The gaps now existing in Canada in this area are tantamount to criminal negligence.
Since ethics underwent a change from a strictly religious dogma to a "social contract" affair, procreation has become a choice rather than a moral or religious obligation. When a choice is to be made, one must have the tools needed to make a sound choice. We are here at a crossroads, but there is practically no means of knowing the consequences of either road. Certain unshakable opponents of abortion will not even admit the fact. In general they also oppose information on sex matters and contraception. They give no choice to future mothers, and the latter must then be in a perilous position: inaction, waiting, fear, indecision.
Now, in this last quarter of the 20th century, we cannot afford to stay undecided. We have to make a choice, and it is the duty of the government to make sure that our choice is enlightened. Therefore, we must emphasize social measures aiming not to favor abortion, but to suppress the need of it. We must table on global measures about population, information on birth planning and contraception. And, above all, because this is the underlying principle to any systematic assistance plan for the human development of families, it is only within a collective adjustment of our family policy that our society will be able to respect individual liberties which all the Canadians think so highly of.
Besides, in spite of all the assertions to the contrary by "anti" groups, experience shows that a global policy of
January 28, 1975

assistance to the human development of the family, such as there is in other countries-I am thinking of the Danish act on abortion, and also of the French act-experience shows that the best way to control abortion is to pass a bill allowing abortion and providing appropriate consultation and assistance services to couples regarding family planning. Both aspects go hand in hand. Therefore I support the statement of the League of the human rights when it says that they cannot admit abortion as a right, but as an emergency measure justified by the right of anybody to health and to the human quality of life, as well as by the right of women to decide on the number of children they want to have and to be helped by society.	[DOT]
I plead for the quality of life, which cannot go with the unbridled population explosion as recommended by some undeveloped countries. I plead for procreation to be a willfull and conscious act, rather than the result of chance. I plead for a morality that, at last, takes into account the psychological and social development of individuals, without which emotional health of the human being is impossible. I plead for measures and services-and here, our responsibility is very important-as I was saying, measures which will insure a better physical, sexual, mental, emotional and social health to all members of a family. I plead for real conditions of well-being and respect of life for children. I plead for the couple.
Mr. Speaker, the proposed amendment to the abortion legislation which we have before us this afternoon is indicative of the malaise in which this debate is taking place. Amendments are moved to do away with the three-physician therapeutic board because the latter, depending on hospitals and regions, is likely to be partial in its assessment of the facts, and especially the physical condition of the mother.
On the other hand, great care is taken to stress in the explanatory notes that social or economical conditions which affect the female person or her family unit must not be taken into account by the qualified medical practitioner when assessing the facts.
Does that mean that the hon. member feels that the advisory therapeutic abortion committee should consider the said criteria of a largely psycho-social nature? That, we are not told. Presently, such is not the case. I for one say that, first of all, the sections concerning therapeutic abortion ought to be deleted from the Criminal Code. It must be clearly established that the committees or other similar organizations must consider the psycho-social reasons that prompted the person-and it is the case for 60 per cent of the requests-to ask for an abortion. And finally, it is essential to set up immediately a government planning and advisory body to which the person requiring an abortion could refer, until a comprehensive family assistance policy is implemented in Canada.
