Mr. Speaker, I support very strongly the presentation made this afternoon on Bill C-219 by my colleague, the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty). His presentation was one of the finest we have heard in this parliament. The member distinguished himself by bringing forward, in the manner he has, a subject replete with controversy and emotion in a way that was
Abortion
shorn of the emotionalism that clouds many minds on both sides of this House on this subject. It is an honour for me to follow his presentation and to speak to one or two points contained in it.
I listened with great interest to the speech just made by the hon. member for Lafontaine (Mr. Lachance). I took it to be a prolife speech. He said he wanted abortions to be prevented in this country. He wants better family planning information made available throughout the country. The hon. member pleaded for the quality of life and for life itself to be truly respected. He spoke of the malaise in this country because of the increasing abortion rate. As I listened to the hon. member, I wondered why he and those of his colleagues who feel as he does did not press for some means to be found whereby this question would be allowed to come to a vote in this parliament.
It is likely that the bill before us this afternoon will meet the normal fate of private members' bills and be talked out. If that should happen, so be it. But let there be at least on record some speeches pleading with the government not to allow the present situation regarding abortion to continue. I myself have spoken to several Members of Parliament who were here in 1969-I was not here then- and who voted for the omnibus Criminal Code amendment which gave us the now infamous section 251 which permits abortion for a wide range of reasons, and they have told me that if they had known then what they now know they would not have voted for the enlargement of the Criminal Code with respect to abortion at that time.
I believe the Canadian people have a right to know where parliament stands on this issue. Obviously there is polarization in the country. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) is attacked by some for being too strict in his interpretation of 251. He is also attacked by those who say he is remiss in his duty to uphold the law by staying quiet while the abortion rate quadruples as a result of the way in which this section has been interpreted.
The Canadian people are confused. I think they need to be led by parliament through an examination of this subject and of the situation which has arisen with respect to abortion since the Criminal Code was amended. The Canadian people deserve leadership from parliament. I think it is scandalous if we are expected to wait until the public mood becomes so definite, one way or another, that we can follow what the public opinion polls tell us is the prevailing mood. I was especially pleased with the speech made by my hon. friend from Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo because he spoke directly to this question of parliament and leadership.
I ask members opposite, particularly members of the government, to allow a parliamentary examination of this subject if through no other device than that of merely allowing Bill C-219 to go to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs after second reading. After all, what is that committee for if it is not to examine the way in which the law is being followed or abused? Let us have an impartial, objective, unemotional examination of what is happening in this country with respect to abortion so that we may not be subject to the kind of thing which is presently happening. For example, the President of the Canadian

Medical Association makes a speech which I can describe as a very unfortunate speech, and then goes on television, using the prestige of her office, to sway public opinion in a manner which I thought was an insult to the medical profession.
In passing, I express the hope that those members of the medical profession who were as indignant at the comments of Dr. Betty Stevenson as I was will speak out, using their names. Let us hear from doctors, because doctors are in a privileged position. The other day the Ottawa Journal carried a letter commenting on Dr. Stevenson's remarks and signed "MD". Who, I ask, is "MD"? I will tell you who "MD" is. "MD" was the pseudonym, the name submitted for publication, by at least ten doctors in the community of Ottawa who took umbrage at Dr. Stevenson's remarks and who wrote without revealing their names. I can only say to those doctors that they were falling down in their duty to give leadership to the Canadian people in this very sensitive area of the right to life.
I want to close on this note. There are so many aspects of the abortion question that it is easy to get lost amid the different arguments-the biological, the medical, the sociological, the ethical, the legal, the demographic and so on. No wonder people are confused. I believe it is the duty of parliament to concentrate on the civil rights side of abortion because this is the side which most directly concerns the law. And is that not our business here-to be making the law and reflecting on the manner in which the law is being followed?
If we look at the abortion statistics since the Criminal Code was amended we see that the abortion rate has climbed from 11,152 in 1970 to 43,201 in 1973, the last year for which statistics are available. Abortions have, in fact, quadrupled in that period; they have reached a point at which they constitute 12.6 per cent compared with live births in this country. This is an alarming situation. Why is the abortion rate climbing so rapidly?
Also, when we look at the figures, we find that in the three wealthiest provinces, British Columbia, Ontario and Alberta, the abortion rates are higher by far than those for any of the other provinces. I will put these figures on record to illustrate my point, and I repeat they are supplied by Statistics Canada. In 1973 the abortion rate in British Columbia was 26.7 per cent of live births. In Ontario it was 18.3 per cent, and in Alberta it was 13.8 per cent. It is ludicrous to suggest it is more dangerous to be pregnant in those three wealthier provinces than in any of the other provinces. It is ridiculous to suggest it is less healthy to be pregnant in those three provinces. It is this kind of question which is bringing the law into disrepute today.
What is really happening is that more abortions are being performed in those areas of Canada where abortion clinics have been set up on a wide scale, because a growing number of women are deciding that if it is not convenient for them to carry their child to term they can decide in favour of an abortion.
I do not want to take up any more time of the House. I say only that the Parliament of Canada cannot much

longer stay quiet or neutral on this subject because we ourselves are divided and expect the people of Canada to look to us for leadership. We have seen this afternoon an example of the kind of leadership that this country needs, and I commend it to the government.

Mr. Speaker, to be fair to my colleagues who would like also to express their views I shall try to be as brief as possible and to omit a few paragraphs.
Very often, Mr. Speaker, I have been asked to take position on the abortion issue. In fact, to be honest, I must say that I do not like to discuss this matter. However, I shall not find it difficult to outline and defend the position I took on this serious problem of abortion. This is a distinction that makes all the difference in the world. A theoretical, logical type of debate referring to philosophy, ethics, biology or theology does not seem desirable nor possible to me. Furthermore, I never use this kind of intellectual approach to abortion-even if it gives rise to lengthy and exciting intellectual discussions for some people-I consider it above all as a concrete, acute and frightening problem that tens of thousands of Canadian women from 14 to 50 are facing each year without any help or hope. And this, Mr. Speaker, I cannot tolerate or consider normal. My position is practical and not intellectual. I do not understand men, and very often some of my colleagues who logically relate their views on capital punishment to abortion. Those two subjects have nothing in common, if not a moral and highly emotional dimension, but their premises are basically different.
January 28, 1975

I think my position is known as I co-signed in 1970 the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada. Under the title "Responsible Parenthood" in the chapter entitled "Women and the Family" and not in the chapter dealing with criminal law, we clearly established the relationship between the self-accomplishment and the slavery of women depending on whether the birth of their children was accepted or acceptable or was a physical or other constraint, sometimes even unbearable. We discussed the happy or disastrous effects of motherhood on women, couples, children, of course, and society as a whole. All this work was based on the many briefs and testimonies received all across Canada during our public auditions. The recommendations of the report to Parliament read as follows:
We recommend that the Criminal Code be amended to permit abortion by a qualified medical practitioner on the sole request of any woman who has been pregnant for 12 weeks or less. We recommend that the Criminal Code be amended to permit abortion by a qualified practitioner at the request of a woman pregnant for more than 12 weeks if the doctor is convinced that the continuation of the pregnancy would endanger the physical or mental health of the woman, or if there is a substantial risk that if the child were born, it would be greatly handicapped, either mentally or physically.
Those are recommendations Nos. 126 and 127.
I think I can confirm that the recommendations are the "smallest common denominator" the members of the Commission could reach. I endorsed them without misgivings. They correspond to a liberalization of our Criminal Code. However, I personally go a little further, and I think that abortion cannot and must not come within the provisions of the Criminal Code.
The facts of pregnancy are often far from what we wish to believe and see. Perhaps one cannot begin to understand until one has witnessed the misery and distress of a pregnant woman who cannot accept her condition, despite all the efforts and help of others. I have often thought that this is the kind of instance where reality perhaps gets to us only through someone close: a friend, a sister, a daughter, a wife, an acquaintance. When faced with human tragedy involving someone, some person whom one must help, great theories vanish quickly and one is surprised, disturbed and shocked to discover the unacceptable and dangerous situation thrust upon women in this country. Indeed, the current provisions of our Criminal Code lead to ambiguity. Besides, I could say the same thing about the section of private Bill C-219 now before us. I repeat that the current provisions lead to ambiguity and however restrictive may be the Code as to the legal aspect of abortion, it is still ten times worse in practice, for it requires bureaucratic procedures and an hospital organization which probably make abortion still more difficult.
We all know about the 1969 amendments to Canada's Criminal Code. It is clear now that one cannot rely on today's legislation to reduce either the number of illegal abortions or the number of deaths or unfortunate results that are brought about: sterility, etc. Any legislation that has more unfortunate than favourable results is bad legislation. Until today's legislation is amended, something like
100,000	Canadian women, perhaps more, of whom a few hundred will die, are bound to transgress it this year. We know all about it in the province of Quebec and even in Canada's metropolis, Montreal, where hypocrisy has
Abortion
reached a degree of absurdity, and I mean to say that it is easier to have the cost of an abortion performed in New York or elsewhere refunded by Medicare than the seek legal abortion as approved by one of our very few hospital committees. Now let us not make a secret of it: if there are many young girls anxious to get an abortion, national statistics in other countries corroborate what we know about this country. Most of the women who want or try to get an abortion are married and already have two or three children.
This leads me to expose those who consciously or not confuse the very serious public debate on abortion. The words "for" or "against" abortion are very inappropriate not to say irresponsible words. Nobody is "for" abortion. There is not one woman in Canada who would want an abortion just like that, on impulse and out of sheer wantonness. Women can give life: they are "for" life, not "for" abortion. However, contraceptive methods that would be absolutely safe and available, that could be used by any woman without any after-effects simply do not exist at the present time. There will be for a long time, surely too long, a great many cases of dangerous or intolerable pregnancies and frequent recourse to abortion.
Movements which are exploiting this problem emotionally and send us an abundant and very expensive publicity financed by sources I do not know, are liable to be accused of dishonesty, and their colour pictures as well as their brochures on the development of the foetus are aimed at handling public opinion. All these militants would do much more for Canadian families by asking their respective provinces to establish family planning hospitals so that pregnancies are the most deliberate and best possible choice.
Moveover, it is very difficult to discuss abortion without going into the much broader problem of birth control. And here, I shall recall quickly the fact that before 1969, for instance, six years ago, such hospitals were technically illegal in Canada. This is a measure of the progress made by the legislators, but when we see the extremely low number of hospitals, about 90, we are concerned about the irresponsibility of governmental authorities, particularly provincial authorities.
Birth control centres should be very varied in their form, as well as in their information techniques and population services. However, they can obtain federal aid only if they request it. In 1972-73, only $991,541 were allocated to this field for all Canada. In 1973-74, this figure increased to $1.25 million. Our own federal government reserves for its part 1 cent a year per woman of procreative age for publishing information on birth control. We should definitely re-think our priorities.
Mr. Speaker, I am nearly finished. My male colleagues often end a conversation on abortion by saying: "Fortunately, this does not concern me. I have nothing to do with this problem!" I always want to remind them that it usually takes two to make a baby. Even though in my opinion the decision concerning abortion involves only the woman since she alone must give birth and, unfortunately, too often raise her children alone, changes in the Criminal Code are the responsibility of the legislators of this Parliament, which includes 96.5 per cent men. As far as such a basic question is concerned, we have no right to let our

January 28, 1975
Abortion
personal fears and the general and vague anxiety created by these times of economic uncertainty lead us into taking reactionary attitudes.
The repeal of the matter of abortion in the Criminal Code, or at least its true liberalization, is an extremely urgent problem in Canada and one which concerns all of us. On this point, I entirely agree with all previous speakers. This issue concerns justice certainly, but it concerns compassion even more. This very beautiful word is often misused. Yet compassion means "to suffer with". In the "Dialogue des morts", Fenelon wrote: "Compassion is love that grieves for the sorrow of the loved one." This is the only valid position as concerns the abortion problem.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance) moved

speechtext:
that Bill C-49, to amend the statute law relating to income tax, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.
He said: Madam Speaker, the purpose of this bill, C-49, is to implement the many important changes in personal and corporate income tax provisions proposed in my
Income Tax
budget of November 18. A number of these amendments form an integral part of the measures put before the House to give effect to the basic thrust of economic policy contained in that budget.
Members will recall that the essential objective of the budget is to deal simultaneously with the twin problems of inflation and slower growth. It is aimed at stimulating increased output and productive capacity, both to lessen inflationary pressures and to maintain satisfactory economic performance. It is aimed at reducing the real impact of inflation on Canadians and sustaining economic growth by moderating the prices of certain particular products, by maintaining real incomes, particularly of those Canadians least able to protect themselves against the rising cost of living, and by helping to stem the erosion in the value of savings.
I might point out to hon. members, in passing, that a number of other countries have also recognized that we must deal simultaneously with the problems of inflation and slow growth, the most recent being the United States' administration.
Several of the measures proposed in this bill, as in other bills giving effect to the budget, will serve a twofold purpose in meeting our objective. For example, the substantial income tax cut proposed for 1975, together with the automatic decrease provided through indexation, will reduce personal income taxes otherwise payable by more than 15 per cent. This will have a significant effect in moderating the impact of inflation on Canadian families and, by sustaining their real purchasing power, will also help to sustain real economic growth.
Similarly the measures to protect and encourage savings, such as the $1,000 exemption for interest, dividend and private pension income, and contributions of up to $1,000 annually to the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, will help both to offset the adverse impact of inflation on Canadians and to provide the funds required to finance the increased capital investment so essential to maintaining the healthy growth of our economy.
To strengthen the position of incorporated small businesses, which form such an important part of our economy, the bill incorporates the proposal first put forward in the May budget, and reintroduced in November, to increase the annual limit on profits taxed at the low small business rate from $50,000 to $100,000, and the cumulative limit from $400,000 to $500,000.
To provide part of the additional revenues we consider necessary to maintain the proper fiscal balance in the months ahead, the bill also gives effect to measures proposed in the budget for increased income taxes, such as the 10 per cent surtax from May of 1974 to April of next year on profits of corporations other than small business, manufacturers and processors, and mining and petroleum companies.
In addition the bill also proposes new rules relating to corporate reorganizations, foreign income and other areas as part of the continuing process of tax reform.
I do not think there is any need to take the time of the House at this stage to elaborate further on the many

amendments to the Income Tax Act contained in this bill covering the areas to which I have already referred.
I would like instead to deal at some length with the amendments relating to the taxation of the production income of the petroleum and mining industries, which have been the major source of controversy.
Since I brought down the November budget there has been a great deal of debate over the whole question of resource taxation in this House, and in the country. A considerable amount of time was also spent during the two-day conference of federal and provincial finance ministers in Ottawa early in December threshing out this same problem.
As I told provincial ministers attending that conference, however, much of the debate has been over issues that, in my opinion, are peripheral or irrelevant. There has been virtually no discussion whatever over what I consider to be the core issue. That issue is what constitutes a fair sharing of revenue from petroleum and mining as between industry, the provinces and the federal government.
During the course of the conference a number of provincial ministers acknowledged that in the end what the dispute boils down to is a matter of dollars, not dialectics. There has even been some passing acknowledgement among opposition members in this House that this is the heart of the issue. But no provincial government and no opposition party has, to my knowledge, yet revealed what it considers to be a fair sharing of production income between industry, the provinces and the federal government.
Before I come to this central question, however, I would like to comment on some of the other issues raised in the debate which, as I have already suggested, are largely peripheral or irrelevant.
First let me deal with the contention that through the resource measures proposed in the May and November budgets the federal government deliberately embarked on a confrontation with the provinces by deciding, unilaterally and without consultation, to disallow the deductibility of royalties, and in the process breached the agreement reached by first ministers at the conference last March.
Traditionally royalties imposed by the provinces have been a flat and moderate charge against a unit of production. It was the provinces, not the federal government, which first took the initiative over a period of several months in radically altering this traditional practice. They did so unilaterally and without prior consultation with the federal government. Through a' wide variety of new levies the provinces took steps to substantially increase their own share of resource production income and, as a consequence, drastically reduced the share going to the federal government. Whatever their form, many of these charges were, in reality, thinly disguised income taxes, and income taxes customarily have not been deductible since Confederation.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) pointed out during the budget debate, the federal government sought without success to initiate a discussion of the whole question of resource revenue sharing during the first ministers' conference last January. In subsequent discussions and letters following that first conference and preceding the

March conference, the Prime Minister made abundantly clear the federal government's concern over the impact of these new provincial resource levies in eroding the federal tax base. He wrote:
We feel that we must preserve the effectiveness of the federal taxing power to raise needed federal revenues. Any action taken or contemplated by the provinces with regard to royalties,
Then he added:
-has to be regarded as being without prejudice to our freedom of action as regards federal taxation.
In the face of this pre-emptive action by the provinces the federal government found itself left with no alternative but to propose measures to parliament aimed at protecting the position of the federal treasury. These measures did not in themselves reduce the return to the provinces. They served only to prevent the provincial levies from undermining the federal treasury. Of course those proposals were first announced to the House of Commons in the budget in keeping with the time-honoured parliamentary practice.
From the train of events I have just outlined it should be apparent that the federal government did not at any time precipitate a confrontation with the provinces, nor did it violate either the letter or the spirit of the agreement arrived at by the first ministers at the conference on March 27. The provinces were fully forewarned before that conference of the federal government's determination to protect its tax base from erosion by new provincial charges. Furthermore, the question of the relationship of federal and provincial resource taxes never formed any part of that agreement, with the result that the budget proposals could not in any way be construed as a breach of the agreement.
Now I want to take up the suggestion that our various calculations on the relative shares of petroleum revenue going to industry, the provinces and the federal government under varying circumstances have been misleading because they failed to take account of the charge imposed on oil exports to the United States. Underlying this point of contention is the strong feeling in some quarters that the full world price should be paid for Canadian oil by consumers both at home and abroad, with the vast bulk of the resulting revenues being shared between the petroleum-producing companies and the provinces in which they are located.
The federal government has recognized for some considerable time that over the longer term an orderly increase in the price of petroleum would be necessary both to promote the development of new, higher cost supplies in the provinces, the north and offshore, and as a means of conserving supplies. But neither the government nor any opposition party in this House considered that the price for domestic oil sold in Canada should be determined solely on the basis of a world price established by a tightly-knit international cartel without any relationship to international competitive forces.
Along with every party in this House, the first ministers at their conference last March recognized the essential need to shield the Canadian people from the harsh impact being felt in other countries due to the abrupt and massive increase that was taking place in oil costs abroad. Members will recall that at that conference first ministers
January 28, 1975

agreed unanimously that a single national price of $6.50 a barrel should be established for a 15-month period to the end of June of the following year. I do not think anyone here would deny that that accord, based as it was on the fundamental principle of a reasonable sharing of the benefits and burdens of Confederation, has been very beneficial for Canada and for the Canadian people.
As a mechanism for implementing this single national price policy, it was agreed by first ministers that the funds derived from the export charge should be employed to cushion the price of high cost oil imported into Eastern Canada, and other oil-related costs. The federal government is not a beneficiary of this charge. In effect it acts only as a conduit for passing these benefits on to consumers in Eastern Canada, and to provinces qualifying for increased equalization payments.
Furthermore, the export charge is relatively short-term in nature, and the revenues produced from it will steadily diminish as the Canadian price moves more closely toward the international price and our exports to the United States decline. The export charge, therefore, is not a significant factor to be taken into account in considering the sharing of production income from petroleum over the balance of the current decade and beyond.
Let me turn now to the constitutional argument, namely, that our decision to disallow deduction of royalties and other similar levies infringes on provincial ownership and jurisdiction over natural resources and, as such, constitutes an attack on one of the cornerstones of Confederation.
As I emphasized in the budget, the federal government does not for a moment dispute provincial ownership and jurisdiction over resources. But provincial ownership and jurisdiction does not in any way preclude the right of the federal government to tax enterprises doing business in Canada, wherever located and whatever the nature of their business.
From our point of view the question of the deductibility of provincial royalties raises a very practical problem, not a constitutional, legal or philosophical problem. We would have been more than happy if we could have achieved the same financial result for the federal government by other means than disallowing the deductibility of royalties. However, the fact is that we could not conceive of any other practical way of achieving that result. I would like to provide the House with a few figures to illustrate this essential point. But before doing so I want to put the matter briefly in some historical perspective.
Over a period of many years, and especially since the second world war, the federal government, and through it the Canadian people, agreed to forgo a substantial amount of revenue from resource companies as a result of generous tax incentives provided to encourage the development of these industries and the provinces in which they were located.
Up to the end of 1973 only a handful of petroleum companies were paying any corporate taxes. Between 1947 and 1953 they paid less than $500 million to the federal treasury, while the provinces collected ten times as much, some $5 billion, through various kinds of levies.
Income Tax
Furthermore, millions of Canadian consumers also helped to foster the development of the domestic petroleum industry under the national oil policy, in effect from 1961 until very recently, by providing a guaranteed market for the western Canadian oil at above world prices. Between the time when the tax reform came into effect on January 1, 1972, and the end of the first quarter of 1974 there was a gradual increase in Canadian petroleum prices. The federal government's share of petroleum production income was running at around 5 per cent, and the provincial share, including royalties and provincial corporation taxes, was running at around 22 per cent.
In April of last year the price of Canadian oil was increased from around $3.80 a barrel to $6.50 a barrel as a result of the agreement reached at the first ministers' conference on March 27. If the existing provincial royalty systems had remained unchanged, the share of production revenue going to provincial governments would have increased to around 31 per cent-the share to the federal government would have increased to about 13 per cent. As a result, the government of Canada on behalf of the Canadian people as a whole would have begun to approach a fairer return from the growing profits yielded by higher prices and the advanced development of the petroleum industry. This prospect was radically altered, however, by the move of several of the provinces to increase substantially their taxes, royalties and other levies on the petroleum companies.
Alberta introduced an incremental royalty which average 65 per cent of the increased price of oil. Saskatchewan introduced a royalty equivalent to 100 per cent of the increased price. B.C. proposed new and heavy royalties on oil, and announced that the British Columbia Petroleum Corporation would appropriate most of any increase in the price of gas.
Now let me go back to my contention that there is no practical way by which the federal government could receive a fair and reasonable share of resource revenue other than by disallowing the deduction of royalties.
If the federal government maintained the existing tax system unchanged, which of course provides for the deductibility of provincial royalties, the interaction of the increased oil price and vastly increased provincial levies in effect before the budget would have drastically eroded the federal corporate tax base.
For the last nine months of 1974 the federal share of petroleum production revenue would have been slashed from 13 to 6 per cent, while the provincial share would have jumped from 31 to 42 per cent. Over the period to the end of the decade the federal share would have averaged only 8 per cent. Industry's share would have amounted to around 45 per cent, and the largest share-47 per cent- would have gone to the provinces.
Suppose, for the sake of argument, we agreed to allow the continued deductibility of provincial royalties but were foolish enough to abolish all other tax incentives extended to the petroleum industry, and taxed the companies at the standard corporate rate. In that case we would still fall far short of achieving what we consider a fair and reasonable share of resource revenue for the federal government. In those circumstances, leaving royalties deduct-

Income Tax
ible but eliminating all other incentives to industry, as some hon. members suggested, the federal share of production income earned in Alberta would be only 12 per cent, while in Saskatchewan it would be no more than 3 to 4 per cent.
If there is any remaining doubt in the minds of hon. members about the drastic way in which provincial action can erode the tax base of the federal government, let me provide another very revealing illustration. Suppose the oil royalty system put into effect by Saskatchewan prior to the November budget were adopted by other provinces. In that case the federal government's share of petroleum income under its existing tax system would have plummeted to less than 1 per cent! By contrast, the provincial share at today's prices would have been at least 60 per cent, and at world prices it would amount to around 80 per cent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I understand it, every other party in this House believes that the federal government is entitled to receive a fair and reasonable share of income from resource companies for the benefit of all the Canadian people.
In an interview in the Financial Post on June 29 of this year, the Leader of the Conservative Party (Mr. Stanfield), clearly indicated his conviction that the federal government has a responsibility to take action when he said:
... if some provinces are trying to take too much or are eroding in a significant, or improper, way the tax revenues of the federal government or the right of the federal government to share in the profits of those corporations.
That stand is very consistent with the view which his government submitted to a federal-provincial conference in November 1963-when he was still premier of Nova Scotia-on the principles of fiscal arrangements between the two levels of government. The federal government must retain a sufficient portion of the tax fields in Canada to enable it to discharge its direct constitutional responsibilities and to assist provinces with low tax potential so as to enable them to furnish a national standard of services to the Canadian citizens residing within their boundaries.

Now is an opportunity for them in this debate to let us know where they stand, because we have to deal with these issues on a clause by clause basis.
The House is entitled to know. Does the Conservative Party subscribe to Alberta's original stand that the federal government-and through it the Canadian people-should be content to receive no more than the 6 to 8 per cent that would be its share if it maintained the resource taxation system unchanged? Do members of the New Democratic Party in this House subscribe to Premier Blakeney's apparent view of what constitutes a fair share for the federal government, something between 1 per cent and 4 per cent? If that is so, now is the time for them to rise and let the Canadian people know how they propose to handle the national politics of this country.
I would like to suggest to members of the New Democratic Party that there is simply no way in which they can reconcile their position in favour of the maintenance of a strong federal government and their support for the share of resource income that would go to the federal government under the kind of tax regime advocated by the Saskatchewan premier. In no way can one reconcile those two positions. It is worth recalling, Mr. Speaker, that the day after the budget last May the then Leader of the New Democratic Party derided the resource taxation proposals as "a laugh". This was Mr. David Lewis, then the hon. member for York South. He said:
Sure, the corporations will complain publicly. Surely they will object to the loss of some of their gains, but I am certain that when their presidents and directors went to bed last night they included John Turner in their prayers.
That is beautiful language, Madam Speaker.

speechtext:
It is vitally important that the companies should be able to earn a return that is sufficient to compensate them adequately for the risks they incur and to generate the funds required to meet the high cost of finding, developing and delivering the resources we will require in the future. It is clear, however, that there is a proper balance to be struck.
In the May budget I proposed changes in resource taxation which would increase the federal share of production income over that which would be yielded by the interaction of the existing tax system and the new system of resource levies established by the provinces.
During the intervening months leading up to the November budget we undertook extensive discussions with the provinces and the resource industries as part of a careful re-examination of our position.
We recognized that the outlook for the future supply of petroleum had become more uncertain and that, in the case of both petroleum and mining, the prospective costs of exploration and development had escalated significantly. For these reasons, therefore, we concluded that it was necessary to ensure that an increased share of production income was made available to the companies to enable them to finance these undertakings.
This brings us to the heart of the issue, namely, to what extent governments should pull back in total to provide industry with sufficient revenue to do its job and to what extent each level of government should pull back.
It is obvious that there is much more scope for adjustment by the provinces than by the federal government. In the case of petroluem, for example, the provinces between 1974 and 1979 would collect $22 billion from royalties and other levies, 53 per cent of production income, while under the May proposals the federal government would have collected only $9.5 billion, 23 per cent of production income.

I dealt with the export tax before the hon. member slid in through the curtains.
Nevertheless, in the November budget I indicated the federal government's readiness to pull back significantly. I proposed a two-stage reduction in the federal corporate tax on petroleum companies from 30 per cent to 25 per cent by 1976, and restoration of the 100 per cent write-off for exploration expenditures incurred by mining and petroleum companies from the 30 per cent rate proposed in May. By comparison with the May budget proposals, these measures would improve the position of the oil and gas companies in 1974 by around $100 million, and the mining companies by $15 million. On balance the resource industries would be about 25 per cent better off in 1974 than would be the case under the May measures.
Over the period from 1974 to 1979, the effect of these November measures would be to reduce the federal share of petroleum production income to 18 per cent from the 23 per cent share that would have resulted from the May proposals. The industry share of production income would increase from around 24 per cent to 29 per cent, and the provincial share would remain unchanged at around 53 per cent. Over the six-year period the federal share of revenues would be reduced from the $9.5 billion that would have resulted from the May measures to $7.5 billion-a
Income Tax
decrease of $2 billion. It should be apparent, therefore, that in both relative and absolute terms we pulled back very substantially.
Members will recall that at the conclusion of my remarks on resources in the November budget I appealed to the provinces to fulfil their heavy responsibility to the resource industries by doing their part to ensure that they obtained sufficient revenue to find and develop the new mineral and petroleum supplies we need for the future.
As I have already indicated on previous occasions, I very much welcome the responsible and responsive decision subsequently adopted by the Alberta government also to pull back substantially so as to ensure achievement of the objective we both share. While it has inevitably taken time, I believe that in the end the two levels of government have acted in that spirit of compromise and co-operation that has served to maintain the strength of confederation over the years.
The full extent to which Alberta plans to draw back is not yet known because the provincial government has announced its intention of consulting with the petroleum industry before determining what reduction will be made in its supplementary royalty rate on existing crude oil production if, as, and when the price rises above the existing level of $6.50 a barrel. Nevertheless, the changes in the Alberta system of levies already announced provide significant concessions, putting an additional $2*/2 billion into the pocket of the petroleum industries during the period from 1974 to 1979.
Taken together the federal and Alberta proposals would increase the cash flow of the petroleum companies by around $4'/2 billion to a total of about $14.7 billion between 1974 and the end of the decade. At the same time their share of production income would increase from approximately 29 per cent to 35 Vi per cent.
I am also pleased that the British Columbia government has indicated its readiness to take at least some modest steps to improve the financial position of natural gas producers in that province. We are happy to co-operate in working out arrangements between the two levels of government that will facilitate this development.
As I indicated to the House previously, I have been giving consideration to the question raised about the possible impact of the new resource taxation system proposed in the budget on the Saskatchewan Power Corporation. It is my understanding that gas acquired by the corporation both from Alberta and from within the province is supplied to Saskatchewan consumers essentially at cost after provision for its own administrative, operational and debt expenses. Assuming that to be the case, no element of royalty or similar levy by the province is involved, with the result that the Saskatchewan Power Corporation should not be affected by the fair market value rule contained in the bill now before the House. Since there has been some doubt regarding the meaning of "fair market value" in specific circumstances, I should like to advise the House that I intend to introduce a clarifying amendment.
From all that I have said, Madam Speaker, it will be evident to the House that in our judgment the federal share of production income that would be yielded by the

proposed new system of taxation of production income from mining and petroleum operations in the provinces is fair and reasonable. The steps taken subsequent to the budget by the provinces, particularly Alberta, also go some way to help ensure that a fair and reasonable share of production income is made available to the petroleum industry. We are co-operating with all three western provinces to establish a rebate program through the collection system that will facilitate an improvement in the financial position of the petroleum companies in a variety of ways.
I recognize, of course, that there are still other important issues relating to petroleum that remain to be resolved. There is, for example, the vital question of the extent and timing of any future increase in the prices of oil and natural gas, a question that undoubtedly will be of paramount concern during the meeting of federal and provincial first ministers in April. Crucial decisions also need to be reached on the over-all fiscal regime that will apply to resources in the frontier areas. While both of these issues are difficult and complex, I would hope they can be resolved satisfactorily within a reasonable time.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is important to consider Bill C-49 in its proper context. This bill is the most important to have arisen from the budget speeches which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) made on May 6 and November 18 of last year.
The bill deals with the law relating to income tax. It is a lengthy bill of 286 pages. It contains 142 clauses. Most of its provisions, however, deal with proposed amendments which are technical matters. They are needed to correct the many imperfections in our income tax law and they arise from the needlesly massive revisions of the law undertaken by the government. In the main the proposed changes had better be dealt with in committee. But there is an important aspect of this legislation that should be fully debated in this House.
It is through the income tax legislation that the government receives most of its revenue-revenue which it, in turn, usually spends. To the extent that such revenue is lessened, government expenditures are lessened. In short, control the government's revenue and you control its spending habits. On the other hand, to the degree parliament permits excessive revenues to accrue to the government we facilitate future excess spending by that government. That is why we, of the official opposition, believe it is important that every member of this House should scrutinize the record of the government, and the record of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), before passing this bill which amends legislation that is so vital and fundamental to government spending plans.
For example, we should ask, has this government handled public funds responsibly and prudently in the past? Are the government's revenue forecasts reasonable? Have ministers done proper planning? Speaking generally, do
January 28, 1975

they even know where they are going? Most important, Madam Speaker, do they really need the taxes which they propose to levy on the average Canadian? The answer is, no. We have a big spending government and, to the degree its gushing revenues permit, it will continue to be a big spending government.
Former finance minister Benson was widely, and in many ways rightly criticized while in office. But, compared with the present finance minister, Mr. Benson showed the height of responsibility in fiscal matters. Look at the record.
In the four years previous to the present minister taking office, budgetary expenditures rose 49 per cent, to a 1972 total of $14.8 billion. In the current four-year period, if we include the Turner forecast as set out in the budget, for 1976 such expenditures will jump by 95 per cent to $28.8 billion. Most alarmingly one finds that personal income tax revenue since 1972, on the basis of the Minister of Finance's own figures, by 1976 will have risen 105 per cent. Considering the 95 per cent jump in government spending and the 105 per cent increase in personal income tax, how can the Minister of Finance state, as he did yesterday in Toronto, when referring to the last budget:
... We have attempted ... to stimulate growth through reductions in personal income and sales taxes, rather than through more inflationary increases in government expenditures.
Later in the same speech the minister had the gall, the nerve, to say this about his last budget:
I moved to inject additional stimulus into the economy in the least inflationary way by cutting taxes rather than by increasing government spending.
What a conversion on the part of a man who has tolerated the highest government spending in history. What an about face by a man who is now Minister of Finance and who has been a member of a government which has spent more money since 1968, the year this government took office, than has been spent at the federal level by all governments since confederation, that is in 100 years.
Did we really see a conversion on the part of the Minister of Finance in Toronto, or was he merely telling his audience what he thought they wanted to hear? If the Minister of Finance is sincere in wanting to curb government spending, if he truly believes taxes should be cut, he has not demonstrated his sincerity to date.
The personal income tax reductions contemplated in Bill C-49 are inadequate. The sales tax reductions, as set out in Bill C-40, and now passed, are unsatisfactory, considering Canada's present economic condition.
The economic outlook for 1975 indicates that the Canadian growth in real gross national product will be marginal, probably not greater than half our capability. Residential construction will fall in real terms by 16 per cent, exports will fall by 3 per cent, and inflation will remain at over 10 per cent. Unemployment will hover in the 7 per cent range. These are not my figures. They are figures prepared by the Institute for Policy Analysis of the University of Toronto, and they are alarming.
If the Minister of Finance continues to take no lead at the federal level to defeat inflation, we may well find that
Income Tax
in future years the 10 per cent inflation rate of 1975 will become the platform for even higher inflationary levels. Here again the Minister of Finance appears to be in the process of a conversion. Dealing with inflation, he now speaks about a program to be voluntarily supported in a national effort to gear down the rate of inflation. To date we have not learned any detail with respect to the program. We have not learned exactly what he has in mind. Instead, he appears to be stalking industry, stalking labour, looking for ideas, holding consultations and discussions.
It may be that the Minister of Finance is working on a prices and incomes policy. It may be that he intends to set some guidelines, or even to propose a social contract concept between the government and the private sector. However, to date he has not indicated what are his intentions.
Perhaps he will be the first Minister of Finance to hold such discussions with the private sector and yet not tell us what he is doing. In short, it may be that these ongoing dialogues are little more than an operation to fill in time. Perhaps the minister is waiting for the learned group of seven, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his six private advisers, to tell him what to do. So far, however, it has not been anything but pretty talk without even a pretty case.
It is time the minister became frank with the Canadian public. At these floating discussion group meetings what guidelines does he propose for price increases? What guidelines does he propose for wage increases? To what extent is he encouraging productivity in our economy? What incentive does he propose to ensure there will be greater productivity? What recommendations is he making with respect to improving Canada's export position? In short, does the minister intend to propose any anti-inflationary program or does he intend to extend three years of drifting with the economic currents to four years of rudderless indecision?
When we review the record of the Minister of Finance we find that his three years in office have been more froth than substance. They have been years of rhetoric rather than performance. Today, he has been Minister of Finance for three years. I do not imagine he is celebrating. Certainly the Canadian people do not have anything to celebrate. During those three years inflation has risen from an average rate of 2.9 per cent in 1971 to a current 10.9 per cent. A dollar today buys 78 cents in goods compared to a dollar in 1972. No one is hurt by such inflation more than the wage earner or salaried employee. His taxes are deducted from source and they keep rising, while the value of his take-home pay remains static.
In the third quarter of 1974 while personal income tax revenue rose a startling 28 per cent there was no real growth in the economy. In spite of this fact the Minister of Finance in his Toronto address yesterday lashed out at labour claiming that at the present time, to use his words:
The major driving force in inflation is coming from the rapid escalation of wage and salary costs as those who work press for increased incomes.
What a startling statement for any Minister of Finance to make.
Let me touch on unemployment insurance. Unemployment benefits paid through that commission in 1974 of

January 28, 1975
Income Tax
over $2 billion equalled the three-year payout before this minister took over from finance minister Benson. In the last three years the UIC has distributed $6 billion compared to $2 billion in the previous three years. The unemployment rate, however, has averaged 5.8 per cent in the Turner years compared to 5.7 per cent in the previous period.
From January, 1972, to the present, conventional mortgage interest rates have climbed from 9 per cent to 12 per cent, while house prices have jumped as high as 50 per cent, resulting in fewer and fewer persons being able to buy homes.
The reasons for our economic plight are easy to discern. Since the present Minister of Finance took the Canadian financial reins there has been real growth of less than 15 per cent, yet government spending has jumped 70 per cent, our money supply is up 56 per cent, and bank borrowings, including personal credit, are 82 per cent higher. Naturally this has produced inflation, inflation at the rate of 28.6 per cent.
Canada, with its abundance of natural resources and primary products, has been able to stand these increases better than could most other countries. We are one of the few developed nations which benefit from a worldwide boom in food and raw material prices. Without such resources Canada would have negative real growth at the present time instead of static real growth.
Canada will not be so fortunate in coming years. The magnitude of the government's ineptitude and mistakes will become evident. World commodity prices are falling as demand lessens. As a result our trade deficit in the current year will widen. Canada will have little real growth in 1975, yet inflation will rage on only slightly below current levels.
For the agile and fast thinkers 1975 may be a satisfactory year. Certainly, no one will benefit from rising unemployment. Some may benefit from inflation. For the majority of Canadians, however, inflation will continue to be a killer. It will continue to rob the pensioner, hurt the wage earner, discourage the young person trying to buy his first home, confiscate property, and it will confuse the investor who won't know which way to turn between recession on the one hand and government induced inflation on the other.
Public confidence must be restored. The Minister of Finance's mystery conferences with members of the private sector are not enough. Lack of candor and a lack of frankness on the part of the government will not restore such confidence.
Perhaps I have been too hard on the Minister of Finance. It may be that he has not been alone in creating our fiscal stew. We have learned of the existence of another economic advisory group in government. I refer to the Prime Minister's group of seven. Perhaps during debate on Bill C-49 we will learn more of the activities of this secretive group. What has been their input with respect to the November 18 budget or the May 6 budget? Clearly there has been some type of artist at work on these budgets. The results have been more impressionistic than realistic.
Could it be the true authors of these budgets are in the Prime Minister's office, or the Privy Council office? In

that event the Minister of Finance is just running the road show. He is Minister of Finance in name, while others prepare the budgets. He simply presents a budget on behalf of the other advisers and then tries to explain their deficiencies. We may in fact have something unique here-a phantom Minister of Finance.
We believe the tax reduction provisions in Bill C-49 are inadequate. They should be explained fully during the committee stage. We hope the Minister of Finance will be able to tell us why he refuses to give a substantial tax break to the Canadian public. They deserve it. It is clear, from his own figures, that he lifted an unnecessary $1 billion from the Canadian public in 1974. That was the year when direct personal taxes jumped a startling 27.6 per cent.
The minister proposes in Bill C-49 to increase the deduction with respect to personal income tax for 1975 and subsequent years by a mere 3 per cent. We believe this is not adequate. The deduction should be increased by a further 5 per cent and we intend to demand to know why it has not been increased by this further 5 per cent as a minimum, when we reach the committee stage. The amount of money which would accrue to the treasury under the present government suggestion, something in the order of $500 million, should properly be left with the taxpayers. If it is left with the government I can assure you, Madam Speaker, that the big spending ministers on the benches opposite will certainly get rid of the money, and the Minister of Finance will once again be obliged to whimper that he has been outvoted at cabinet meetings when he tries to impose restraint on government spending. Such government spending will be inflationary itself.
As I indicated in the debate on Bill C-40, we were disappointed that the government did not completely remove the sales tax on building materials. With housing starts slumping so dramatically it is hard to understand why the minister, or, for that matter, the group of seven, refused to eliminate the building material sales tax entirely. We are told it would have cost $380 million in lost federal revenue, but I can assure hon. members that it would have meant the saving of tremendous administrative costs, and, more important, it would have given housing a much-needed boost.
We believe the minister should explain why he refuses to index capital gains in response to inflation. The University of Toronto study to which I have referred, states:
Fiscal drag, which inflation would have generated with a tax transfer system without indexing, would have been sufficient to plunge the economy into recession in early 1975 unless offset by discretionary fiscal changes.
Indexing was an idea advanced by us. We intended that indexing should apply not just to incomes but also to the capital gains tax. We want to know why the minister has not seen fit to act along these lines. We find that the bulk of the minister's so-called tax concessions are the result of indexing, a Conservative proposal, and the partial removal of the sales tax on building materials-another Conservative proposal. The minister has adopted our ideas but he has carried them only part of the way. If the minister must copy our ideas let him do it accurately and fully.

The hon. gentleman spent a great deal of time dealing with the royalty question. I want to assure him that we are rigid in our view that the clauses in Bill C-49 dealing with the federal government's proposed encroachments into provincial royalty fields with respect to natural resources are unsatisfactory in their present form, and unacceptable to our party. Speaking generally, we hope the minister and the government to which he belongs will give up their tactic of confrontation in this important area. My hon. friend from Don Valley will have more to say on this matter during the course of the debate.
In the present inflationary period we believe business people should be given more equitable tax accounting treatment in respect to the carrying of their inventories and the replacement value of their assets. Again, this subject will be dealt with more fully during the committee stage.
Others in my caucus will be dealing with the inadequacies of Bill C-49. I refer, for example, to the housing measures which form part of this legislation. My hon. friend from Kingston and the Islands will deal with this aspect of the subject. My hon. friend from Prince Edward-Hastings will deal with our deteriorating export position and the failure of the 1974 budget to have any effect whatsoever on that worsening picture.
In conclusion may I say we agree with the minister's budget statement that, at the present time-
-the fiscal stimulus should come primarily from a further cut in taxes rather than from an additional increase in expenditures. I believe that tax cuts can help reduce prices and costs directly or indirectly and thus slow down the upward momentum of inflation. An indiscriminate or excessive increase in expenditures would exacerbate the pace of inflation.
We only hope the minister will match his words with meaningful deeds. It is not good enough for the government to say it will try to keep the increases in expenditure down to 15 per cent as the Minister of Finance has indicated. Let there be no doubt-if we in this House give the government excess revenue, the government will spend it whether the Minister of Finance tries to stop it or not.

subtopic: HEALTH-INABILITY OF DOCTORS TO COPE WITH INCREASE IN TROPICAL DISEASES
HEALTH-INABILITY OF DOCTORS TO COPE WITH INCREASE IN TROPICAL DISEASES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) in the House tonight since I am once again raising the question of the necessity for establishing a school of tropical medicine in Toronto where there is a concentration of tropical visitors. In view of the great number of immigrants who came to Ontario in particular during the last few years, many from areas where cholera, intestinal parasites and infections run rampant, I sometimes wonder whether we living here realize the danger presented by these diseases.
In one area I visited some years ago I saw 19 infants die in a 24-hour period of gastro-intestinal infection. New diseases brought to Canada include whipworm, Chinese liver flukes, roundworm, and tapeworm. The great majority of immigrants, as I say, come to Ontario, with Toronto being the chief recipient. Many come here illegally, unknown to the authorities, and some perhaps even work in restaurants in that city.
Jet travel has enormously increased the spread of tropical disease. In the meantime we have not kept pace by training doctors or providing the lab facilities to handle the problem. For instance, two years ago 416 travellers returned from foreign countries with some infection. Since we have no school of tropical medicine we do not have enough doctors trained in this field to cope with the situation or to recognize such disease when they meet it. Consequently hundreds of these people run around in ill health and infect others.
I had a personal experience of a professional man who had visited the Middle East. When he came back he was seriously ill for some months. I got suspicious when he came to me that he may have had a tropical disease. We did stool cultures, he was treated and cleaned up. This cost a lot of money and health care.

January 28, 1975
Adjournment Debate
What do we demand of immigrants who work in restaurants? The first thing we demand is an X-ray. But how many of them have ever had a stool culture? I believe that when the Royal party visited Canada there were a few stool cultures done in some areas of Toronto, but why not a stool culture for everyone who handles food? Is it because we do not have the necessary facilities to do this that these are not done? This is the advice I have received.
As I have said, travellers are not checked on return from abroad. Nor are they advised by travel agents of the possibility of picking up some of these diseases in the places they visit. To indicate the rate of increase in such diseases, I understand there were around 350 infections in 1967; there were over 3,000 in 1974. We not only lack beds to treat these people, we lack the trained personnel. As a result it is likely that these diseases will continue to spread. As I say, many immigrants work in restaurants, and we owe it to ourselves to make sure they are given a stool examination.
I think it is only fair to mention that I understand a troop of players who were playing in Asia, as well as in Poland and Russia, returned to play at Stratford. They were found to have an infection which was nipped in the bud, and the troop went on to play at Stratford as scheduled. I also wonder about hockey teams, and other people who have gone over as spectators. How many of them have come back and are now carrying chronic infections? I wonder how many of them have been treated, and how much that treatment cost.
The jet age has introduced instant communication with all people of the world, most of whom have much lower hygienic standards than ours. This means we should use extreme caution in maintaining our health standards which are among the finest in the world.
I would suggest that the federal government require all immigrants, as well as individuals who return from travelling abroad, to report to local medical officers of health. I have not made reference to the hundred or so new cases of leprosy in the United States, or the fact that Bing Crosby, that well-known crooner, picked up a fungus while on safari in Africa which required an operation, following which he was released from hospital just a few days ago.
All of these things have taken place, but how much has the federal government given in aid to fight these diseases and solve these problems? How long will it be before the government establishes a department of tropical medicine in Toronto, where most of these cases occur, as a centre for all Canada where these cases can be treated?
By following this suggestion we would not only be keeping up our high standards of medicine and health care in this country, but also we would be preventing these diseases and cutting our OHIP health costs.

Madam Speaker, I always listen with great interest to the contributions to our debates by the hon. member, not only because of his experience in the House but obviously because of his professional expertise in the field of medicine.
The hon. member has talked about a certain problem which is and should be of concern to all of us, namely, the problem in respect of tropical diseases. In a previous

question directed to me by the hon. member he referred to "the galloping increases in tropical and parasitic diseases which has now gone beyond the ability of doctors to cope with."
It is true that in the last decade the number of reported cases of tropical diseases has increased, with the province of Ontario registering the biggest increase and the largest number of cases. It should also be noted that I am advised that no cases of the quarantineable diseases of small pox, cholera, yellow fever and plague were reported during the 1963 to 1973 period.
Observers feel that this increase is due to the increasing numbers of persons now travelling around the world and visiting Canada, and to the many Canadians returning home from abroad, such as tourists, missionaries, Canadian public servants, military personnel and representatives of agencies like CUSO and CIDA-I could go on and on.
I should like to say a word about the hon. member's question regarding precautions taken to make sure that travellers get proper medical advice and vaccination. Travellers proceeding abroad have recourse to current information provided through 23 medical travel information offices across Canada operated by the medical services branch of my department. In addition, my department publishes a comprehensive guide on immunization requirements and recommendations for international travellers. I would be pleased to provide the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) with revised versions, if he so wishes.
As for precautions taken to ensure that travellers are checked for proper vaccination when returning to Canada, travellers, returning from a country where certain diseases are prevalent will be asked for proof of vaccination against such diseases upon arrival at the place of re-entry to Canada. If such proof is not provided, vaccination is made available to them.
The hon. member also asked about what steps are being taken to increase the number of doctors in the field of tropical and parasitical diseases. The hon. member knows that the training of doctors falls within the provincial domain. The practice he has suggested is certainly one I have had in mind, and I intend to discuss it again with my colleagues.
I would like also to refer the hon. member for Simcoe North to the recent formation of the Tropical Medicine and International Health Division of the Canadian Public Health Association, which has resulted in an increased awareness and attention among health professionals to the diagnosis and understanding of tropical diseases.
In conclusion I would like to say that the government is aware of the problems posed by increasing numbers of international travellers and visitors to Canada. The Department of National Health and Welfare is consulting with the Department of Manpower and Immigration on measures that could be taken to protect the health of Canadians without impeding the free flow of travellers and visitors to Canada in the context of the present review of immigration legislation and policies.
January 28, 1975

CONSUMER AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY RINGS AND LIDS FOR MASON JARS TO PRESERVE FOOD-REASON FOR LACK OF PROTECTION FOR CANADIAN MANUFACTURERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak about the shortage of lids for wide mouthed Mason jars in western Canada. I do so because I do not believe that the urgency of the question which I have put in the House regarding the shortage of such lids was fully appreciated by Mr. Speaker, by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) and his department, by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and his department, and by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and his department.
The shortage of these lids in western Canada is very real. It developed first in 1973, but became a real problem in 1974. This matter must be solved now if we are to have a good supply of these lids in western Canada in 1975, because it is necessary to supply the steel plate to the manufacturers now to make it possible for the lid manufacturers to supply them in time for the canning season.
I realize that there are many people in eastern Canada who have not experienced this shortage and do not know how this whole matter could be solved. They believe that there is no urgency until the canning season comes around. However, if we are to have these supplies, now is the time to take action.
When I say that the shortage experienced in western Canada was real I should like to illustrate it by telling you a story of a constituent of mine who had 200 jars in his basement. During the canning season last summer he found that he did not have one lid for any of his jars. He spent some time and money calling the brokers, the wholesalers, across western Canada. He called every city in western Canada. Then he started calling eastern Canada, but he did not find any lids for his jars, until he was able to contact a broker in Montreal who had some of them. But then the problem was how to get them. It was not very easy.
The reason the shortage has developed over the years is that the suppliers of lids for wide mouthed Mason jars were in the United States. There are two suppliers in the U.S.-Kerr and Ball. They were able to supply the market because lower prices kept manufacturers from eastern Canada out of the western Canadian market.
There are two manufacturers in eastern Canada, Ber-nardin and Anchor Cap, but Canadian manufacturers cannot compete with those in the United States because of
Adjournment Debate
the policies of the government. Of course when a shortage of steel plate was developing in the United States in 1973-74, manufacturers there cut back on supplies to Canada. Manufacturers in eastern Canada did not have inventories of steel plate so they could not make the lids because they were still working on the quotas for the past three years.
My appeal is principally to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, but I include the Minister of Agriculture because of the nature of the products being canned. He has been telling Canadians to produce food, but what is the use if the people of western Canada cannot get lids when they want to can the food they grow? Even the home gardener can help fight inflation by growing food, but he must be able to get the equipment when it is time to do the canning.
So I appeal to the department to do something to ensure that manufacturers in eastern Canada get the steel plate they need to manufacture the lids for western Canada where they are needed. We should not have to rely on foreign products; naturally when their production is low they cannot supply our demand.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY RINGS AND LIDS FOR MASON JARS TO PRESERVE FOOD-REASON FOR LACK OF PROTECTION FOR CANADIAN MANUFACTURERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the officials of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce have been advised that the Canadian manufacturer of lids for the wide-mouthed Mason jars has recently set up a second assembly line to increase their production.

A Canadian steel mill has also assured a sufficient supply of tinplate to cover this increased production which should satisfy all areas of the Canadian market.

At the present time, the tariff in that field is 17.5 per cent (most favored nation). The problem lies in the preference shown by a sector of public consumption for an American product rather that in the lack of protection given the Canadian manufacturer. When the American producer withdrew from the Canadian market, the Canadian manufacturer, who was producing at full capacity for his market, was unable to meet the sudden increase in the demand.
